I understand that the principal feature of this Bill is the creation of share warrants. Would the hon. minister kindly explain?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
The memorandum attached to the Bill explains it pretty well, I think. It says:
A share warrant Is a share certificate transferable by delivery without any record of such transfer being made in the books of the company. The warrant usually provides that when dividends are declared by the company, an advertisement thereof setting out the rate and time of payments must be inserted in certain newspapers, and also that the dividend coupon attached to the warrant may be cashed at certain banks. On the appearance of an advertisement of a particular dividend the holder of the warrant may then present the coupon for that dividend and obtain payment thereof. Share warrants may at any time be exchanged for ordinary share certificates. This section was first enacted in Great Britain in 1867 and is taken without substantial change from section 37 of the present Imperial Companies' Act. It is similar to sections 61-69 of the Ontario Companies' Act. The main object of the section is to enable a company to issue a kind of security which is probably the most important
dealt in on the European exchanges. This kind of security is particularly popular in France with small investors, and the French law renders share warrants more easily dealt with. There is no change from the Imperial Act except where the necessities of our Act demand verbal changes.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.
Mr. CODERRE moved the second reading of Bill No. 189, to regulate the manufacture, testing, storage and importation of explosives.
Would the minister kindly explain?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
In 1908 the attention of the Government was directed to the many fatalities that had occurred through explosives in railway camps and mines throughout the country. Dr. Haanel, Director of Mines, considered it advisable to have Mr. Desborough, one of His Majesty's inspectors of explosives, look into the matter. Mr. Desborough visited the provincial Ministers of Mines, and various construction camps and mines throughout the country, and made a report containing some very valuable data. In 1909 a conference met in Ottawa at which were present Dr. Haanel, Mr. Desborough, representatives of mine owners and manufacturers of explosives, and delegates from some of the labour unions in the country. The conference listened with great interest 10 the memorandum read by Mr. Desborough, and, acting on the suggestion contained therein, Mr. Templeman, ex-Minister of Mines, drafted a Bill which was brought down in the last session of the old Parliament. The Bill reached the committee stage, and ten clauses were passed, but it was found impossible to get the Bill through that session. The present Government realize that this is a very important matter, and steps were taken last year to bring a Bill before the House, but on account of the length of the session it was impossible to do so. It is the desire of the Government to get this Bill through this session. The officers of the department and Mr. Desborough believe that by the enactment of such a law the number of fatal accidents through explosives would be considerably lessened, although of course the danger can not be entirely eliminated. To give the House an idea of the risks undergone by those who use explosives in mines and on railway construction work, I may

quote some figures taken from the Labour Gazette. In the year 1912-13, 92 fatal accidents occurred in this country through explosives; 19 in mines, 47 in railway construction, and 26 in other employments. We believe that if this law had been on the statute book many of these accidents would not have occurred.
Does it in any way affect provincial laws?	*

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
This Bill, before being introduced, into Parliament during the session of 1911 by Mr. Templeman, was examined by Mr. Newcombe, the Deputy Minister of Justice, and he gave the following opinion with regard to it:
I have examined the draft Bill respecting explosives which you left with me a few days ago and return the same herewith.
The point which you particularly submitted for my consideration was as to the constitutional authority of the Parliament of Canada to enact such a Bill. The Bill contains a variety of provisions, many of which are doubtless of a general character, while there are others, such as for instance, those providing the precautions to be observed in the manufacture of explosives which have a local aspect. In respect to such provisions, and possibly in its entirety, the Bill covers debatable ground, but I should anticipate that the Bill if enacted by Parliament would upon the principles of construction of the British North America Act already laid down by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, be upheld as competent Dominion legislation. If the Government consider that it is expedient for the peace, order and good government of Canada to enact such a measure, I see no sufficient reason to advise that they should refrain from promoting the Bill for any reason based upon doubt of the constitutional authority of Parliament to enact it.
I may add that the Minister of Justice concurs in the view above expressed.
Mr. Newcombe had some doulbt as to whether clause 11, as it originally appeared in the Bill, came within the jurisdiction of this Parliament. But this section will not be found in the Bill at the present time, as, at the suggestion of the present hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty), it has been struck out.

Motion agreed to, Bill read the second time, and the House went into Committee thereon, Mr. Blain in the Chair.
On section 2-interpretation:
Are there any inspectors at the present time, appointed by the Department of Mines, for the purpose of looking after explosives?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: No, there is at present no law.

I called the attention of roy hon. friend the other day to a very serious fatality which took place at Beloeil two years ago at a manufactory of explosives, when, I think, ten people were killed. Coming and going between here and Montreal, my hon. friend may see, on lie Perrot, another manufactory of explosives. I do not know what manufactory it is, but it is close to the track of the Canadian Pacific railway and the Grand Trunk railway, and it is common talk among travellers when trains are passing that a fatality may occur at any time. Sparks from the engine may cause an explosion, which would be most serious in its consequences. I beg to call the attention of my hon. friend to this and to remind him that if his inspectors do not see at once that this manufactory is removed from near the railway tracks the Government will be held responsible. I do not say the Government will be held responsible in law, but the Government will certainly be held morally responsible. It is located at a very dangerous place. We have already suffered in our province from two or three fatalities, and I think the time has come when such a danger should be removed.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Is my hon. friend speaking of the manufactory on lie Perrot?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
It belongs to the Canadian Explosives Company, I am told by Mr. Hudson of the department. My hon. friend will find in subsection (j) of section 19 that the Government will have power by regulation to act in cases such as this. The subsection provides that:
The Governor in Council may make regulations-
(D governing the establishment, location and maintenance of factories and magazines, and the manufacture and storage of explosives.
Will this Bill be retroactive?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
An Order in Council
can be passed regulating such a case as that which has been mentioned by my hon. fr;end.

It should be very
clearly stated that the section is retroactive. I would like to hear from my hon. friend the Minister of Justice on this point.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I see no reason why it should be retroactive. We cannot make it

an offence to have had a magazine where it has been, but we can pass a regulation determining that in future no magazine shall be allowed to remain within a certain distance of railway tracks without the law being retroactive. From the passing of the regulations the existence of magazines in such places will be prohibited.

I do not wish to injure the company at all, 'but I think in the public interest my hon. friend should not allow this manufactory to be maintained right beside the tracks. A spark from a locomotive might cause an explosion and consequent disaster. There have been explosions at Isle Perrot, Hull, Beloeil, causing loss of life. This powder mill on the railway track near Vaudreuil is a constant danger to all who have to pass in that vicinity.

Section agreed to.
On section 3:
This Act shall not apply to the Department of Militia and Defence or the Department of the Naval Service.
Who regulates the carriage of explosives on railways?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
The Board of Railway
Commissioners is empowered to make regulations.	*

I am told that some
railway companies take great risks and that explosives have been carried even on passenger trains. The most stringent regulations should be enforced.

I can quite understand that these departments should be excepted, but I would like to know if there are any regulations governing the carriage and storage of explosives belonging to the Militia and the Naval Service Departments.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: These departments have their own regulations which are given effect to.

There should be regulations in these departments as stringent as those which apply to mines. In the mines we have experts who understand explosives and even under the present law accidents in Nova Scotia, where mining is carried on to a greater extent than in any other province, are comparatively few. In other provinces forty per cent of the injured in mines are injured through explosions while in Nova Scotia it amounts to only one per cent.
On section 4-explosives prohibited unless authorized:

Is it the intention of
the department to pass regulations declaring what are explosives?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Yes.
On section 7-licenses:

Will this section if passed
do away with the necessity which exists at present of applying to the different provincial authorities for certificates to establish powder magazines in any locality ?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
The provinces will still legislate within the scope of their powers. This will not apply to cases already provided for by the provincial law, but to other cases which evidently would fall under the jurisdiction of this Parliament.
Mr. DEVLIN': Section 7 of this Bill provides:
The minister may issue licenses for factories and magazines, and no one shall manufacture, either wholly or in part, or store explosives except in licensed factories and magazines.
In the Revised Statutes of the province of Quebec, article 1269 reads:
Every person keeping a magazine for the storage of powder, or who sells or holds for sale any quantity of powder, must obtain from the collector of provincial revenue a license to that effect.
Article 1270 provides:
Powder magazines shall be constructed in the manner and at the place determined for each such magazine by the Lieutenant-Governor in Council with the consent of the council of the municipality within which said magazine is situated, and no license shall be granted for keeping a powder magazine unless such magazine be constructed in conformity with the authority of the Lieutenant-Governor in Council.
Article 1268 enacts:
* Powder magazine ' means every building used for the storage or keeping of any quantity of powder more than twenty-five pounds in weight.
It appears to me there is a direct conflict between the provincial regulations and the regulations which we are seeking to pass now. If this section 7 be passed, then any person wishing to keep a powder magazine will have to apply to the federal minister, and when he comes to the province of Quebec to build that magazine he will find that the permit he has received from the minister is practically useless, because he is confronted with sections 1269 and 1270 of the Quebec law. He will find further that, under the British North
38G4

America Act, section 92, subsection 16, among the matters assigned to the control of the provinces are:
Generally all matters of a merely local or private nature in the province.
I would call the minister's attention to the fact that a powder magazine located in the province of Quebec is entirely under the provincial law which I have just read, and it should not fall under any law or regulation of this Parliament. I would point out also that the parties most interested in this legislation are the municipalities concerned, and the minister is taking away all their protection.

My hon. friend will
notice also that in certain municipalities they have certain regulations on this subject, and it seems to me that when a company wishes to operate a powder magazine hr a powder factory it must comply with those regulations.

They must first, as I understand it, get the permission of the municipality before they can even apply to the Lieutenant Governor in Council. Section 1270 of the Quebec law reads :
"Powder magazines shall be constructed in the manner and at the places determined for each magazine by the Lieutenant Governor in Council, with the consent of the council or municipality within which such magazine is situate.
The municipalities are well protected now, but I think that under the law proposed by the minister they would lose that protection.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There cannot be any question of the right of the province to require licenses for businesses of this kind. But that is given them under power conferred upon them for the" purpose of raising a revenue-the power to issue licenses. But we are dealing with the question of importation, manufacture and storage of explosives with a view to meeting dangers that present themselves equally all over the Dominion generally, the dangers that attend the presence of explosives. There is certainly no intention to interfere with such regulations as, under a provincial authority, the municipality may be authorized to make for its own special protection, but rather a general provision that the provincial authorities may regard as supplementary. If necessary, we might add to this Bill a clause specifically providing that its requirements shall not obviate the necessity of complying with any local regulations.
[Mr. Devlin "|

I would suggest that the minister add some such words as these in section 7:
The minister may, subject to provincial laws and regulations, issue licenses-
And so on. That would cover the difficulty.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That might mean that we could not issue any licenses. What is contemplated is that the party shall have the two licenses-from us and also from the province. The province has the right, by means of its license, to collect revenue, while this is not a revenue measure but is for general protection. Un-
12 noon, questionably, the province has power to make regulations or conditions upon which its license shall issue. I think that probably the better way to do would be, not by adding something to this particular clause but by another clause declaring that the provisions of this Act shall not so operate as to relieve any person from the obligation to comply with the requirements of local laws on the subject.

But there is more than that in it. This Bill is intended for the protection of the public. The local legislatures, in Quebec at all events, have also that in view. They provide that no powder magazine shall be established in any locality except with the consent of the municipal authority. There are some municipalities in which it would be very dangerous to have a powder magazine established, and therefore the provision subjecting the matter to local consent seems wise. It would be .better that we should provide that before a powder magazine is established anywhere the consent of the municipality must be obtained.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The object is not to put us in a position of interfering with the provincial law. The suggestion of the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) had also presented itself to my .mind; but it appeared to us that to put a clause in this Bill requiring the consent of the municipality might subject our law to the suggestion of interference. We could hardly undertake to deal with special local conditions from the point of view of the protection of a particular municipality. I am inclined to think that if that were the sole purpose, then the whole affair would be a local matter, to be dealt with by the provinces. But what we were trying to deal with were the general oon-

ditions that exist everywhere, regardless of the presence of municipalities, leaving to the provinces their power and right to deal with special requirements in special localities. For instance, it was suggested that we should put into this Bill a provision that there should toe no powder magazine within a fixed distance of a town or village. But after consideration, we thought that it would be more proper to leave to the municipal authorities, acting under the authorization of the local legislature, the determination of what distance from the town a factory would be considered dangerous, because what might be necessary with regard to one village or town might not be, for one reason or another, necessary with regard to another. As I have said, there is no intention and no desire under this Act to relieve any person of the obligations imposed upon him for the protection of the public. What we want to make is a law that will be of general application where the province may fail to legislate or, at all events, of general application to protect the public of the Dominion against the dangers connected with this matter. As I have suggested, It seems to me that 'any possible objection would be overcome if there were added to this Bill a general provision stating that nothing in this Act shall so operate as to relieve any person of any obligation of that nature imposed upon him by the laws of the province or by the municipal authorities acting under the law.

I understand that under
the provisions which my hon. friend suggests putting in, section 1271 of the law of the province of Quebec, to which my right hon. frieind the leader of the Opposition referred a moment ago, will be protected. It is as follows:
A municipal council desiring, for valid reasons, the removal from within its limits or from one part of its territory to another, of an existing powder magazine, shall have the right to obtain such removal upon payment to the company or person owning the magazine, of an indemnity to be determined by arbitrators appointed by the interested parties, subject to the decision of the provincial treasurer.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is a provision giving power to a municipality to enforce removal from one place to another for the protection of the people of the municipality. The added clause may easily be so worded as to preserve that provision, as well as similar dispositions made by a provincial authority or by a municipal authority authorized by the legislature.

I wish to draw attention to subsection g of the Interpretation Act, which is as follows:
Magazine means and includes any building, storehouse, structure or other place in which any explosive is kept or stored, other than at or in and for the use of a mine or quarry in a province in which provision is made by the law of such province for the efficient inspection of mines and quarries.
It seems to me that this 'section excludes the inspection of explosives in the mines in the province of Nova Scotia, because in that province we have an efficient law for the inspection of mines and quarries. In the short time which I devoted to the Revised Statutes of Nova Scotia this morning, I could not find that we have any laws dealing with the inspection of explosives that are used in or about or around these mines. The minister will readily see that if the Act remains as it is, it will exclude inspection of explosives in and 'around the mines in the province of Nova Scotia and I do not think that that would be desirable.

I would suggest to
the hon. member that in all Coal Mines Regulation Acts, it is provided that no explosive shall be stored in any mine. This section, so far as I can read it, will not prevent the provincial Government of Nova Scotia from passing such regulations as the hon. member refers to.
I understand that very well.

The Coal Mines Regulation Acts usually deal w:tb the use and storage of explosives in mines, and there is nothing in this section which interferes with the passage of such regulations by the Government of Nova Scotia.

I understand that. My point is that perhaps the Government will say that it is the intention to exclude the mines in Nova Scotia. If that is the intention and they are doing that under this Act, all well and good; but this Act, notwithstanding that we have not efficient inspection of explosives in that province, will not apply there. I agree with the hon. member from British Columbia that the Government of Nova Scotia may have regulations and may pass very stringent law?; but I want to find out if it is the intention of the department to exclude from its operation the mines in the province of Nova Scotia. That is the effect of this subsection as I read it.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend alluded to the use of explosives in mines and to the inspection of these explosives. The words * use of explosives ' have been eliminated as far as possible from the Bill with a view to preventing conflict of authority where provisions have already been made under the Provincial Mines Acts regulating the use of explosives. On railways, canals or other construction work not so governed federal Orders in Council will be issued to provide for the proper use of explosives, so that adequate protection will be given to the men employed and also the general public.

The word ' magazine ' is defined here and it excludes from the provisions of this Act the storage place of explosives in and around a mine where there is an efficient inspection by the legislative authorities of the province of such mines and quarries. Thus the place where those explosives would be stored around a mine in Nova Scotia would not be called a magazine at all, and would not come under the operation of the Act.

I think the power of inspecting the conditions under which explosives are stored in and about the mining industry of our province is vested in the general inspector of mines, in the general power that is contained in the Mines Regulation Acts. I know, as a matter of fact, that in all the mining districts especially prepared magazines exist in and about the mines. I was going to ask him whether or not this Act had been submitted to the mining authorities, that is the executive authorities, of the different provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: It has
And what was their position in regard to it?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Hudson, one of the officers of the department, went through all the provinces to meet the ministers of mines of the several provinces. He saw Mr. Duncan, the deputy minister, in Nova Scotia, who approved of the law submitted to him, that is substantially the law as it is before the committee to-day.
I am inclined to agree with the hon. member from Cape Breton that the Act will not apply to Nova Scotia in regard to mining.

In connection with the definition of 'magazine,' it certainly does not apply to the mines of Nova Scotia. Has Nova Scotia been purposely exempted

or have the officials, in drafting the section, unintentionally exempted Nova Scotia from the Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I do not think that this section particularizes Nova Scotia; it Tefers to all the provinces.

If I understand correctly, the hon. member contends that this does not interfere with the provisional regulations in regard to magazines around mines, but that the exemption might empower a colliery company to erect a magazine that would be in conflict with this Act. Is that the idea? I agree with the hon. gentleman that provision should be made that no colliery magazine should be erected unless it conforms to the federal statute.

It is exempted from the statute as it now reads. It is the intention of the department to exempt the magazines, storage places of explosives around mines, from the operation of this Act, or is it not? If you have good reason for the legislation as it stands all very well, but I wish to know if a mistake has been made in the drafting of the Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I do not think so.
Was it the intention of the minister to exempt mines?

Around all collieries and mines there is a daily storage magazine, which must be provided for, wherein a certain amount, only enough for the 24 hours' use, is allowed to be stored nearer towns or habitations than is allowed for in this federal statute.
My trouble is that the laws of Nova Scotia do not cover the matter at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Then, of course, the subsection will not apply.

That is what I say, that in Nova Scotia, even if we have no law at all that requires inspection of explosives, we have a law which is for the efficient inspection of mines and quarries. The Minister of Justice follows me in that? And therefore the word ' magazine ' will not cover any province where there is an efficient inspection of mines and forests, but no inspection, efficient or otherwise, in regard to explosives. This is a very technical point, probably.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am not quite clear that I grasp the point of my hon. friend. I

understand that what he suggests is that powder and explosives used in connection with mines in Nova Scotia would be exempt from any inspection at all under the operation of this Act, combined with the provisions of the provincial Act. Is that the suggestion?

Will the minister follow me while I read the interpretation of the word ' magazine '?
' Magazine ' means and includes any building, storehouse, structure or place in which any explosive is kept or stored-
Then comes the exception:

other than at or in and for the use of a mine or quarry in a province in which provision is made by the law of such province for the efficient inspection of mines and quarries.
-not for the efficient inspection of explosives, but for the efficient inspection of mines and quarries. If there is no law in the province of Nova Scotia in regard to explosives, the storage of explosives around mines would not be covered by the word * magazine '.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think that objection is sound, and we could cover the case by adding after the word quarries in the twelfth line, the words ' or of explosives used in connection therewith.'

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I beg to move that the words ' or of explosives used in connection therewith be added after the word * quarries in the twelfth line on page 2, section 2.
Motion agreed to.

I would like to ask the minister as to the condition of inspection in the province of Ontario. Has Ontario an efficient inspection or is it the intention that this law shall apply to the province of Ontario?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I have a letter here from Mr. Miller, provincial geologist for Ontario, regarding explosives, in which he says:
The Mining Act of Ontario only regulates the storage and use of explosives at the mines. There is no regulation regarding the manufacture or statistics to show the amount used.
The manufacture of explosives is a matter of trade and commerce, and as the explosive remains in the form of a commodity which is open to purchase and sale, it is subject to the supervision and jurisdiction of the Dominion Government. As soon as it is brought for use on the mining property, regulations passed by the provincial legislature govern.
It has been felt for some time that the Dominion Government should bring in legislation respecting the manufacture and sale of
explosives in Canada, in view of the numerous accidents resulting from explosives.

What I had reference to was not the use of explosives at the mines, but at the works; say, at a quarry. I would like to know whether we shall have to rely on this Bill for guidance in this matter, or whether there is a law in the piovince of Ontario regulating the use of explosives at the works. I speak of this matter because I have personal knowledge of what is being done; in fact, I am interested, and I think this is the easiest way for me to find out just what the law is on that point. By the way, in the definition of explosives I see no reference to the word ' rack-a-rock,' a very common explosive used in the quarrying of stone. I am unable to determine from the definition, either special or general, whether rack-a-rock is covered.
Is it in the shape oi rockets ?
Yes; it is in the shape of a Roman candle.
I think it would be covered by this definition.

It may be. Rack-arock is practically a non-explosive unless interfered with, and I do not think there is any danger at all from it in storage. It is regarded as a very harmless explosive, and very easily handled. I never heard of any accidents resulting from the use of it. It is used very extensively.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
In answer to the hon. gentleman's first question as to the storage and use of explosives in connection with quarries, I believe, after reading Mr. Miller's letter that this Bill would cover that point, and I think it is also covered by the Ontario regulations. In regard to my hon. friend's other question, rack-a-rock is manufacured by a Sherbrooke company. I have a letter in reference to this Bill written by Mr. White of that company. It will show the reason of a certain amendment which will be found in clause 7. The letter is as follows:
I represent two companies, the principal one of which is the company which manufactures an explosive known as Rack-a-Rock. This explosive has a great many advantages over any of those manufactured by the trust, one of the principal reasons being that it is absolutely harmless up to the very time of its being used. It consists (when shipped from the factory) of two parts, a solid and a liquid, the first being in the form of a fine powder. These two substances can be shipped by freight or express In the same manner as ordinary merchandise,

Inasmuch as until they are mixed in the proper proportions, they are absolutely non-explosive.
The consumer is able to purchase Rack-a-Rock in this form in a great many places where it is very difficult to obtain dynamite, owing to the great danger of transporting the latter. Under the proposed Act, you will see section 1, subsection (e) says:
'Factory' means and includes any building, structure or premises in which the manufacture or any part of the process of the manufacture of an explosive is carried on, and any building or place where any ingredient of an explosive is stored during the process of manufacture.
Section 7 provides:
'The minister may issue licenses for factories and magazines, and no one shall manufacture, either wholly or in part, or store explosives except in licensed factories and magazines'.
I am afraid that under the wording of these two sections it might he held that the place where, for instance, a farmer wishing to blow up stumps mixed the solid with the liquid would be held to be a factory and consequently he would be unable to do it except under the conditions provided for by the Act. An interpretation of this kind would put both of my companies out of business. My clients tell me that at a meeting of the explosive manufacturers and the late Government, when it was contemplated to draft an Act, they were promised that the Act would be drafted in a most elastic form to begin with. Under the Act as drafted there is little or no elasticity at all. I am told that the English Act contains a clause under which, by Order in Council, an explosive may be declared not to be an explosive within the meaning of the Act.
The Bill has been amended to meet the cases referred to by Mr. White, and this amendment will be found in subsection 2 of section 7 as follows:
2. Notwithstanding any provisions contained in this Act the Governor in Council, upon the recommendation of the minister based upon the report in writing of the deputy minister accompanied by certificates from the chief inspector and chief chemist of explosives approving of the nature of the components and of the final explosive product, may allow the inexplosive component parts of an authorized explosive from licensed factories and magazines to be assembled and blended at or near the point of use and such place of blending shall not be deemed a factory or magazine within the meaning of this Act.
I think I understand it.

I understand that, while you might have an explosive that was not dangerous, such as Rack-a-Rock, it would be treated either in transportation, in manufactories, or in magazines, just the same as if it were very dangerous. My hon. friend has just read a letter from the attorney of the Rack-a-Rock Company, Mr. White, and I understand that he refers to the regulations in England as to explosives. The regulations in England provide for different grades of explosives, that is,

grades are established not according to the explosive force but with reference to the amount of danger of such explosive in transportation. In Canada and the United States there are different kinds of explosives. Some of them are very powerful, but they are found to be absolutely without danger while in transportation. Some others are less powerful, but are very dangerous if you transport them, and very dangerous especially in the case of concussion. Others cannot be exploded unless by the use of detonators or percussion caps. I do not know whether it would not be well to provide in our law for a certain class of explosives; that is, apply very stiff regulations to some of them, and to be a little more generous with regard to others. I agree with my hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson) in that respect.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Does not the hon. gentleman think that this point might be met by paragraph A of section 18 concerning regulations?
The Governor In Council may make regulations-
(a) for classifying explosives, and for prescribing the composition, quality and character of explosives.

Yes, but this would apply to the terms of the certificate to be given to the different classes of explosives. I would like to ask the minister by what process or procedure the regulations of the Bureau of Explosives are made to apply in this country. I understand that these regulations, although I do not question the merits of them, are made and modified in the United States, and that we have no control whatever over them. If you want to deal with a railway in regard to the transportation of explosives, they will always refer you to the regulations made by the Bureau of Explosives. I would like to know if these regulations are applicable to this country as the result of an agreement between the railway companies, or if they come under the Railway Act or any regulations made thereunder. I have never been able to elucidate this point.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: In conformity with the Railway Act, the Board of Railway Commissioners have issued regulations for the transportation of explosives.

But these regulations are the same as the regulations made by the Bureau of Explosives which emanate from a United States body. What control

have we over those regulations in the way of making or modifying them?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: The Bureau of Explosives is an American body located in New York. It has its own regulations, but they do not apply here.

If you apply to a
railway company they will tell you that you have to comply with the regulations of that American body. I do not object to these regulations, but I would like to see a procedure of some kind emanating from this Government so that we would have some control over the regulations. I do not dispute the merits of these regulations, but it is awkward to have to comply with regulations that we have no control over whatever.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I do not know that our people should be forced to follow those American regulations unless they are applicable to merchandise shipped from a point on the other side of the line. As far as transportation in this country is concerned, we have our own regulations passed by the Board of Eailway Commissioners under the Eailway Act.
On section 8-permits for importation:

This section will possibly have an effect not contemplated by the framers of the Act. In the interpretation clause it says:
-and includes fireworks, fuses, rockets, percussion caps, detonators, cartridges, ammunition of all description.
Then, section 3 says:
The minister may issue permits for the importation of authorized explosives.
That, it seems to me, would include cartridges for small arms and prohibit the importation of cartridges even by tourists, without a permit. This would work a great hardship. In subclause (j) of the Interpretation Act, safety cartridges mean cart-rages for gun3, rifles, pistols, revolvers and other small arms, of which the case can be extracted from the small arm after firing. 1 would suggest that the words * other than safety cartridges ' he inserted in clause 3 after the word ' permit ', so as to make it read:
The minister may issue permits for the importation of authorized explosives, and no one shall import any explosive into Canada without such permit, other than safety cartridges.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
There is no objection to adopting that suggestion.
Section as amended agreed to.
Is it the intention of the Government to appoint local inspectors at centres where explosives are very much used?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: That seems to be a good suggestion, but I cannot say now if it is contemplated by the Deputy Minister of Mines.
An official at Ottawa would not be in a position to inspect explosives lin the mines of British Columbia or of Nova Scotia.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I will consider that.
Before the third reading of the Bill I would like the minister to give due consideration to section 20.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I move that the Bill be
amended by adding as section 27:
Nothing in this Act shall relieve any person of the obligation of complying with the requirement of any license law, or other law, or by-law, of any province or municipality, lawfully enacted with regard to the storage, handling, sale, or dealing with explosives, nor of any liability or penalty imposed by such law or by-law for any violation thereof.
Amendment agreed to.

A serious accident
occurred some years ago at Essex Centre in connection with railway carriage of explosives. I am unable to say just now what the provision in the Eailway Act is with respect to that, but I have in my hand a memorandum which I shall pass to the minister and ask him to consider it before the Bill is finally disposed of.
Bill reported.
At one o'clock, the House took recess.
The House resumed at three o'clock. MONTEEAL HABBOUB COMMISSION.
On motion of Hon. J. D. Hazen (Minister of Marine and Fisheries), Bill No. 191, to provide for further advances to the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal, was read the second time, and the House went into Committee thereon, Mr. Blondin in the Chair.
On section 1-short title:

I am in sympathy with this legislation brought down by my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. I am glad to hear that the members of the Harbour Board are back to work after their



visit to the various ports in England. When I remarked upon their absence a few weeks ago, my hon. friend, I hope, understood that I did not wish to reflect upon their conduct, because I am bound to say that generally speaking these commissioners are following in the footsteps of their predecessors, and everybody knows that their predecessors administered most efficiently the work carried on in the harbour of Montreal. The hon. gentleman has himself declared on various occasions that if it had been possible for him to retain their services he would have been only too pleased to do so. I understand that the season of navigation of 1913 was marked "by several important works carried on in the harbour of Montreal. Some work has been done in connection with the harbour railway line from Molson's creek to Racine pier. My hon. friend will probably be able to give us a synopsis of what has been accomplished in that direction. Two permanent transit sheds on the Tarte pier have been completed, also elevator No. 2 and its conveyor system in the central part of the harbour. I would like to know what addition^ have been made to elevator No. 1, and what area of reclaimed land has been provided in connection with the dry-dock and the shipyard. 1 understand that last year new quay walls of standard crib-work, substructure and complete superstructure have been built. My hon. friend will be able to tell us briefly what work has been done in this connection. I should like to know also what is the mileage of railway track in connection with the harbour proper and how far the tracks will be extended this year. I understand that the commissioners have removed some artificial work at Moffat's island, and that there has also been carried on the construction of what is called the industrial wharf at Point aux Trembles. Is that industrial wharf to be used by a private company, or is it for the general use of the public? I understand that two sheds on the high-level shore wharfs, sections 24 and 25, are under construction. My hon. friend will be able to tell us if they are going to proceed this year with the work on those .sheds, and whether, in order to expedite matters, they will work during the winter as well as during the summer months. My hon. friend might give also some details about the electric hoist on the Alexandra pier and the paving on the wharfs. Is this work completed, and if not, 
when is it intended to be completed? There are some wooden piers still left in the harbour of Montreal. I would like to know if it is the policy of the department to transform these wooden piers into concrete piers. I would like also some information with regard to the additions and improvements to the construction and operating plant With regard to the dredging of the harbour, I would like my hon. friend to give me the pay-list and to tell me how many men are employed, and how the materials are purchased.
Everybody knows that the harbour of Montreal is possibly the most important point in our whole transportation system. Being at the head of oceanic transportation, it has become practically, de facto, the national port of Canada. A few figures will show its importance in connection with our whole transportation system. The total quantity of grain handled during the last eight years by the Montreal Harbour-Commissioners elevator system, exclusive of the grain handled by the Grand Trunk and other local elevators, shows what im proved facilities have accomplished. I quote from the Montreal Daily Mail of a few -weeks ago. This address was made on the occasion of the re-election of Mr. Andrew Allan. 'In it he referred to the report of Mr. -Arthur Surveyer, a member of the Canadian Society of Civil Engineers, upon the water levels in the port of Montreal. Mr. Allan said:
Last year I had occasion to refer to the probable lowering of the water in the river, as a result on the proposed Chicago drainage scheme. I now call your attention to a report by Mr. Arthur Surveyor, dealing with this matter. I might state that the federal Government have appointed a commission, consisting of Dean Haskell, of Cornell University; Mr. Porneret, superintendent of the Ship channel, and Mr. Stewart, chief hydrographer, to inquire into and report on the whole matter.
In his report on the depth of water in the St. Lawrence channel, Mr. Surveyer says:
The lowest water occurred in November. 1911, when the level receded to less than 28 feet in the so-called 30-foot channel. It is evident that we are still far from the 35-foot channel and, with the lowest water plane steadily receding, it will take probably more than dredging before a 35-foot channel is obtained.
Mr. Surveyer goes on to eay that he is convinced that the low water plane has subsided in the last forty years anywhere *from two and a half to three feet, and that this fall has practically all taken place in the last twenty-five years. He thinks the three causes of the subsidence are the deforestation of the St. Lawrence basin, the enlarging by dredging of the controlling sections of the river, and the diversion towards the Mississippi river by the Chicago main drainage canal of a large volume of water which formerly passed to the sea via the St. Laiwrence river.
I have read carefully the report pre-2444
pared by Mr. Surveyer, and it is appalling to think that the river St. Lawrence may show further decreases in water level, so that possibly the interests of Montreal may be endangered and navigation between Quebec and Montreal may -suffer seriously. I hope my hon. friend can give the House the benefit of his latest information on the subject and give some heart to the people of Montreal. The intelligence that the two new Allan liners, the Calgarian and the Alsatian, cannot come up to Montreal has created a sensation in shipping circles not only in Montreal but the country at large. After the millions and millions^ that have been spent in equipping Montreal harbour, and dredging the channel between Montreal and Quebec, it would be a thousand pities if this strategical point in our transportation system should now be jeopardized. I do not wish to delay the business of the House any longer, and I simply offer these remarks in order to get some assurance from the hon. gentleman that under his care the harbour of Montreal will be well looked after.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I will endeavour to give my hon. friend, as far as I can, the information which he asks regarding the Harbour Commissioners, the work they did last year, what they propose 'doing this year, and, generally, the information he is very properly seeking from me at this time. My hon. friend has very properly referred to the great growth that has taken place in the business of the port of Montreal. It is in order to continue that work, and to provide further facilities for the port that this Bill has been introduced. The purpose of this Bill is to provide a further advance to the Harbour Commissioners of $9,000,000 to defray the cost of additional facilities that have become imperative by reason of the very great expansion of trade at that port, which is the great entrepot of Canada. The development has been very rapid indeed, as may be understood by referring to the revenues of the commission. In 1909 the total revenue derived from all sources amounted to $687,772; in 1912, it had increased to $1,049,311; and for the year ending December 31, 1913, $1,361,964; and, as my hon. friend pointed out, during that period there has been an enormous increase in the total quantity of grain handled by the commission, increasing from 565,355 bushels in 1904 to 43,349,291 bushels handled in 1913. The increase in 1913, over the grain handled in 1912, was between 17,000,000

and 18,000,000 bushels, which is an indication of the great improvement that has recently taken place in the facilities for handling grain at that port.
What are the prospects at present?	(	|

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
It largely depends on the
harvest in the West.
I understand that there is more grain there now than they can handle.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The present facilities will be able to handle that grain. As to the quantity that will be taken out during the year, that depends largely upon the crop that is produced in the Northwest during the present season. We are all glad to know that the prospects for a bountiful harvest are very good indeed. The increase in traffic in 1913 was particularly gratifying, but with additional facilities the growth will be even more marked. It is anticipated that with the extra facilities that are being provided the revenue of the harbour at the close of 1917 will reach the $2,000,000 mark, and that is without the imposition of tonnage dues on shipping. The various rates charged by the commission compare more than favourably with those charged at competitive ports in the United States. 1 might read a short extract from the report of the commissioners and one or two extracts from the report of the old commission bearing on this matter. In this year's report the commissioners say:
Notwithstanding the marked depression in trade in the commercial world during the latter part of the season, due to which it was not expected that the tonnage of the port would show great increase, it is most gratifying for the commissioners to be able to announce that the past year has been a record one, as far as shipping is concerned, returns eclipsing by far those of any previous year, as may be seen from the statements appended hereto, showing respectively, for the past ten years.
I have here the last report made by the old commission, Messrs. Stephens, Ballan-tyne and Geoffrion, and I think it might be well to place one or two quotations on ' Hansard ' for the information of the House. On the first page of the report the commissioners say:
It is perhaps pardonable to restate here that the development plan authorized by the Canadian Government in the progressive enlargement of her seaport facilities at Montreal, has met with the approval of the highest authorities on transportation.
To quote the words of Calvin Tomkins, commissioner of dock and ferries of the port of

New York: ' I believe at the present time, while suffering from the disadvantage of ice obstruction in winter, Montreal nevertheless affords the best example of modern seaport organization.'
In point of monthly volume of business, the port of Montreal takes its place as the second largest port in North America. Without imposing tonnage dues upon the ships, with a tariff of charges one-half of what existed twenty-five years ago, with a handling cost on all her through business reduced 50 per cent in six years, the port of Montreal though only at the inception of its development and far from realizing its ultimate economic possibilities, is able to pay out of a modest revenue all charges of maintenance, running expenses and the interest on every dollar invested in its development.
Canada's national port is, therefore, being developed by money borrowed from the national treasury and upon which the current rate of interest is being paid out of the revenues from the port's business.
Its boundaries have been extended, and the people of Canada now own, in fee simple, 16 miles of water front on either side of the river, untrammelled by a foot of vested interests.
Not alone has an attempt been made to meet the requirements of the great shipping interests in the development of port facilities, but the great railways of Canada have been afforded access to the ships and sheds; the cartage companies have been provided with accessible means of reaching the merchandise warehouse within the harbour limits; while plans have been laid for the creation of an industrial harbour that will afford to all great industries taking advantage of the facilities of rail and water access to their own establishments on an economic basis that will bring power to the prestige of the port.
There has, therefore, been achieved, with a measurable degree of success, a solution of one of the biggest problems which transportation presents, in the co-ordination of rail, river and road traffic, all meeting at a point of interchange, with possibilities of assembling cargo with economy and dispatch.
Passing over to page 249, I might read this, under the heading of General:
Though something has been done to equip the port of Montreal in a manner befitting its importance as the head of ocean navigation, it must be remembered that many problems of great import yet remain to be worked out. In carrying on this work it will be wise to maintain the authority of the port executive in a manner which will permit of all interests using its facilities receiving equal and fair treatment. The administrative staff must understand that upon loyal service and merit alone depend their positions and advancement, and that no outside authority can appoint, promote or dismiss them.
The report is a very interesting one and would repay reading by gentlemen who are interested in the development of the great port of Montreal:
Some years ago the question of providing port facilities at Montreal was referred to a board of consultative engineers. In 1909 this board submitted a report outlining a definite programme of harbour improve-

ments and in the following year legislation was obtained authorizing an advance on account of this programme of $6,000,000. Immediately thereafter plans, specifications, etc., were approved for work estimated to cost $5,242,207.
In 1912 authority was obtained from this Parliament for a further advance of $6,000,000 and subsequent to this, plans, etc., were approved estimated to cost the whole amount of $12,000,000.
What is the debt of the port now?

Harbour Improvements.
A successful construction season, no serious accidents in the port, satisfactory labour conditions and the best season on record with regard to the operation of harbour facilities.
The Harbour Commissioners' railway line was completed to high level along the river front from Molson's creek to Racine pier.
Two permanent transit sheds were finished and opened for traffic on Tarte pier.
The Harbour Commissioners' elevator No. 2 and its connecting conveyer system to all the berths in the central part of the harbour, was operated during the whole of the season with perfect success.
Harbour Commissioners' elevator No. 1, situated in the most favourable position in the harbour for receiving and delivering grain was fully operated during the season, although an addition of one and a half times its present storage capacity was being constructed.
The dry-dock site, providing a large basin for the floating dock 'Duke of Connaught' and a large area of made land for the shipyard, was advanced almost to completion.
New quay walls of standard cribwork substructure and concrete superstructure were completed, having a total length of over 2,200 lineal feet and 2,000 lineal feet partly constructed.
Railway tracks to the extent of about four miles were constructed and an additional one mile improved and relaid.
The removal of the artificial works at Moffat's island was greatly advanced and its ameliorating effect on the St. Mary's current towards the close of the season was very marked.
One of the important items of new work commenced was the construction of a large industrial wharf at Pointe-aux-Trembles.
Another new work commenced was the construction of two new transit sheds on the high level bulkhead wharfs, sections 24 and 25.
A new electric hoist, with bridges, connecting with the upper stories of the sheds on the Alexandra pier was constructed during the season.

Important items of paving on the wharfs were completed and the roadways were put in a very much improved condition.

Important additions and improvements were made to the Harbour Commissioners' construction and operating plant.

The commission was composed of Dean Haskell who has had large experience in that work on the Mississippi and other large rivers in the United States, W. J. It was hoped that the report would be ready for discussion in Parliament this session, but the work was more complicated than expected, and the report will not be ready before next session. We will then have scientific data which will enable us to decide what should be done. If it should be found that the work going on in the ship channel is lowering the level of the water in Montreal harbour, then the question of constructing compensating works to hold back the water will have to be dealt with promptly, because it affects the trade of Montreal, which is a matter of great importance to the Dominion.

The explanation of the hon. gentleman is very satisfactory. What proportion of the work in Montreal harbour is done by the commissioners themselves and what proportion by outsiders ? Are tenders called for all the work which is not done by the commissioners ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
All the work is done under the direction of the commission, but for the erection of the last sheds they called for tenders and awarded the contract to the lowest tenderers. The last elevator was built on the same principle as that adopted by the Canadian Pacific railway in constructing its elevators. They get a reputable firm of elevator-builders to do the work for the cost of labour and material, and above that a commission for their services. The former commission built one of the elevators in the same way. I doubt very much myself whether it is the wisest course to follow. The Quebec Harbour Commissioners recently asked for tenders and made a contract for a lump sum, and I think perhaps the result may be more satisfactory.
I talked the matter over with Mr. Ballan-tyne, who is a sound business man, and he believes that the system gives splendid work and is in the end more satisfactory, and the fact that a great corporation like the Canadian Pacific railway, which conducts its business on most approved lines, builds its elevators on the same principle, is no doubt a strong argument in its favour. All the work in the harbour is d^ae by the commission, with the exception' of that part of the St. Lawrence channel which runs through the harbour, and that is charged against the appropriation for the deepening of the St. Lawrence channel.
The debt of the harbour of Montreal is at present $19,000,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
How much will it be if this legislation passes ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They probably will have spent this money in four years from now and the debt then will be $28,000,000.
Will this be enough to finally equip the port of Montreal?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not think it will. If the country continues to grow we will have to be working all the time at the port of Montreal. The progress of this country wiil to a great extent be measured toy the volume of the business in the port of Montreal. If we have only sufficient facilities for doing the business of to-day, then if the country develops these facilities will have to be increased. I have no doubt that whatever Government happens to toe in power the commissioners will be asking Parliament to make provision for advances so as to keep the harbour at Montreal abreast of the times. I sincerely hope that will be the case.

We shall all be glad to see that happen. I would not, however, like to see the idea go abroad that the Government should toe responsible for all the expenditures at these ports. In improving the port of Montreal we increase the value of every house and every business stand and every piece of property in the city, and the city of Montreal should bear some part of the burden. I understand that at present that is the system adopted in Montreal, and so far I am in accord with it. We are borrowing money and lending it to the Harbour Commissioners, and they pay interest at the rate of three and a half per cent on the loan. I think that is the proper policy. We sometimes hear people advocating that the Dominion at large should bear the expense of equipping what are called the national ports, but that is not the policy in vogue in Great Britain. The harbour trust in Glasgow looks after the equipment of the port in that great city, and it is one of the best equipped ports in the world. The port of Glasgow does not depend upon the Government to sustain it, and the trade of the port pays the interest on the money expended. I am not objecting to the present Bill; it is largely in the line I would advocate, and I simply want to place myself on record in favour of a policy by which the trade of the port of Montreal should bear the greater portion of the expenditure necessary in order to provide for the necessities of that trade.

If I mistake not the
harbour of Montreal is the only harbour in Canada that pays the interest on its debt.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is the only port that is self-sustaining. When the Government constructs wharfs in other harbours the dues on these wharfs are collected under the Harbour Masters' Act and they go into the consolidated revenue of the country. The port of Montreal is absolutely self-sustaining. On every dollar that is advanced by the country the Harbour Commissioners, out of the revenues of the harbour-elevator charges, shunting charges and other items of revenue-have paid the interest.

It is not altogether selfsustaining, because we loan them the money at three and a half per cent, and we are paying more than that.
On section 3-interest on debentures:

Following the line of the remarks of my hon. friend from Guys-borough (Mr. Sinclair), the Minister of

Marine and Fisheries may know that action was taken lately by the city of Montreal against the Harbour Commissioners for the payment of taxes. So far the Harbour Commission has always contended that it, being a commission receiving its power from the Crown, was not liable for taxes. I understand that action was taken and judgment .rendered, Mr. Justice Weir declaring that the Harbour Commission was not liable. Has there been an appeal from that judgment, or has the city of Montreal agreed to accept it?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I understand that it is the intention of the city of Montreal to appeal from the judgment of Mr. Recorder Weir, who decided that the commissioners' property is not liable to taxation. It certainly seems to me that some action will have to 'be taken about the matter if the decision should ultimately be that the property is liable to taxation. It has never paid a dollar of taxation in the past, nor has any attempt been made to levy taxes upon it. While, in a sense, this is the property of the Harbour Commissioners, it is public property in the broader sense of the term, and it would be a monstrous thing, it seems to me, if this Parliament should be asked to make these large appropriations for the port of Montreal and for the enlargement and improvement of the harbour, and then find itself faced with charges to a very large amount-for it would reach a very large amount-for taxes. I understood from the previous Board of Harbour Commissioners that they discussed this matter with the civic authorities, those authorities took the position that they could not do otherwise than impose taxes upon the Harbour Commissioners' property, but that 4 p.m. they are quite willing, if the courts decided that the property was subject to taxation, themselves to apply to the Quebec Legislature for an Act exempting it from assessment. I understand, however, that that is not the attitude of the present civic government in Montreal. That being so, the matter is still in our hands. We are not obliged to make advances to the Harbour Commissioners, and I think we should carefully consider the matter before making advances, and ascertain whether the civic authorities intend to make us pay large sums in taxation. Every citizen of Montreal with whom I have spoken about the matter feels that it is not right that the property should be asked to pay taxes, but that it should be

regarded the same as any other property belonging to the Crown.

On section 1:

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The purpose of this Bill is to authorize a loan to the Harbour Commissioners of Quebec of $2,000,000 to continue the plan of harbour improvements which was commenced under the authority of the legislation of last session. It will be recalled that during the last session authority was obtained for an advance of $3,500,000 to the commission. Immediately following the passage of that measure plans for a comprehensive scheme of harbour improvements were prepared under the direction of the commission, which, in turn, received the approval of my department. In carrying out the work contemplated by this scheme some $2,960,363 was expended up to the end of March last. This left a balance unexpended of $539,637 available for the operations of the present season. Up to the present time very satisfactory progress has been made with the work undertaken by the commission, and * it is confidently expected that before the expiration of the present year there will be available at Quebec accommodation that will substantially assist the growing need of shipping at that port. One of the most important items of the scheme of harbour improvements is the construction of a first-class modern elevator with storage capacity of 1,000,000 bushels. This elevator, including a complete electric power plant, is now practically in readiness to receive grain. Substantial progress has also been made with the extension of the pieTS at the Louise embankment which, when completed, will afford much needed berthing accommodation for the additional ocean steamships coming to the port.
As the result of what the commission has been able to accomplish in the short time that they have been in charge of operations, a very satisfactory increase in the traffic, as evidenced by the increased revenue, is to be noted. For the year 1912, the gross earnings of the harbour were $126,131.39.

For the year ending the 31st December last, the earnings had increased to $176,020.80, exclusive of an annual rental the commissioners propose to charge for the site occupied by the new Dominion Immigration building of $50,000. When the improvements contemplated by the proposed loan are completed there is every reason to believe that the increased traffic will yield ample revenue to provide for operating and interest charges.

speechtext:

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes. I may say that the old debt, exclusive of the loans of last session and this, is about $5,415,722.

That is very satisfactory.
I wish to call the attention of my horn, friend to a statement which he made not very long ago, and which was received with great satisfaction by Canadians at large, namely, that, as far as possible, any ship or any material required by the Government in connection with shipping would be purchased or built in Canada. I was very much surprised to learn that the Quebec Harbour Commission had recently placed orders abroad for a large crane, a large dredge, a floating grain elevator, and a steam tug. The value of this equipment will amount to several hundreds of thousands of dollars, in fact, my hon. friend, in answer to a question which I put lately, stated that this will entail a very large expenditure. All of this equipment could have been constructed at different Canadian works, at Levis, near Quebec, or at Montreal, at the Vickers' works, or on the Great Lakes at Collingwood, or elsewhere. There

are several structural steel companies in Canada fully prepared to accept an order for the construction of such vessels. There is a plant at Levis, the Davey plant, one at Kingston, one at Montreal, one at Colling-wood, one at Toronto, one at Port Arthur, capable of building the whole of these different appliances. There are more than a dozen engine builders and boiler builders in Canada fully equipped to produce the engine plant and boiler plant required, of the highest possible quality. In fact, we know that lately possibly the largest grain carrier ever built was launched at Colling-wood on the Great Lakes. As a Canadian and a moderate protectionist, I cannot see why this Government of high protectionists should go abroad to get the appliances and the ships and the dredges and the engines and boilers required for the Harbour Commission of Quebec, or any other commission in the country. We have the Canadian Westinghouse Company, the Canadian General Electric Company, each of them having an output equal to the largest British companies, each fully prepared to deliver all electrical appliances required on the shortest notice, of the very highest quality, not to speak of several other electrical works in Canada. Every dollar's worth of material and every day's wages that have been put on, the building of these harbour appliances abroad for the harbour at Quebec could have and should have been provided in Canada. It is true my hon. friend may say that after tenders were called he found that the prices in England were a shade cheaper than the prices in Canada, but it has always been the policy of this Government and of former Governments to give the preference to Canadian firms. You must bear in mind the Customs duties which enter into the account, and in that way you can give our Canadian firms the preference. The Marine Department has recently announced, through a statement of my hon. friend in the House, that it is the policy of the Dominion of Canada to place all orders of the Department of Marine, for shipbuilding, in Canadian works. Does this rule not also apply to other public works, and will not the Government state that instructions will be given to all harbour commissioners and all bodies having authority to place orders for marine or other appliances to be used in harbour improvements or other public works, that all such orders must be given to Canadian manufacturers. We have the Westinghouse Electric Company at Hamilton, the Steel Company of Canada, also at Hamilton, the Bridge Works
[Mr. I.einioux. [
at Hamilton, the General Electric Company, the Poison Iron Works at Toronto, the Col-lingwood Shipbuilding Company at Colling-wood, the Western Dry Dock Company at Port Arthur. So, not going outside the province of Ontario, these appliances could have been supplied by the firms which I have already mentioned. These works, with the capacity for employing 50,000 workmen, are curtailing their operations and discharging their workmen because of lack of orders, while these public bodies, like the harbour commission, are sending public money abroad to employ foreign workmen in the same occupations. The Vickers Company, of Montreal, could have filled the whole order in its own works for these harbour appliances.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not think they could then, as their works were not ready. They could now.

With all due deference, I met the other day one of the members of the firm, who had read the answers given to pay questions on the Order Paper. He said that he felt very sorry that his firm had been forgotten in the distribution of orders and that the Vickers in Montreal could have supplied all those appliances. At all events, I simply call the attention of my hon. friend to the announcement made some months ago that in future his policy would be to give the preference to Canadian firms as regards Canadian ships, and, generally speaking, Canadian appliances for our Canadian public works and for the use of the harbour commission, etc.
There is another point about the harbour commission in Quebec. Of course we all have a great deal of confidence in Mr. Price, the chairman of that board; but some facts have come to public notice lately which lead me to believe that it would be a good thing if Mr. Price could be at the office every day because these facts would lead to the belief that the administration is somewhat lax. I shall give an instance. The Harbour Commission purchased lately a quarry at a place called St. Nicholas in the county of Levis, just across the river. The property, three acres by five, approximately, was purchased on the 2nd of April, 1913, from a gentleman by the name of Jules Giroux. The price paid was $4,500. This Jules Giroux had purchased the property from a man named Desjamin Demers, on the 29th of March, 1913, for $2,000; that is to say, in less than a week a profit of $2,500 was realized on a property which

had been bought just a few days before foT $2,000. That may be a small amount, but it enables one to judge of the other things that are being done by the Harbour Commission. I do not wish to detain the House at any length because every minute of out time probably costs $2,500, but I simply leave this fact with my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and the hon. gentleman who is leading the House, the Minister of Public Works; $2,500 made out of the people of this country in less than five days. Surely there is a nigger in the fence.
In the quarry, you mean.

This man, Jules Giroux, who sold the property to the commission, states in the deed of sale that he received no consideration, that he is only a go-between ; but it is known that he is a brother-in-law of the son of one of the Harbour Commissioners, Mr. Gravel. Far be it from me to impute motives, but I say to my hon. friend that he had better tell Mr. Gravel, that his son has a brother-in-law who is rather costly to the country, because in four days he was able to shave off a nice little profit of $2,500. If we must judge Mr. Gravel in big things as he has been acting in small things, I say to my hon. friend be careful of this $2,000,000 that you are advancing. That is a large amount of money, and I say: keep your eye wide open, Mr. Minister. I hope my hon. friend will read the Riot Act to Mr. Gravel and tell him to stop all such nonsense. This little graft of $2,500 is unworthy of the Quebec Harbour Commission. I am sure that if Mr. Price had known of this deal he would not have sanctioned it. On the whole, the explanations of the hon. gentleman are quite satisfactory, and I leave him with this little grab of $2,500.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I may say to my hon.
friend that he and I agree entirely as to the policy of having Canadian ships built in Canada, and to show how that policy is being carried out I may say that all tenders that are now being asked for, for the construction of ships for the Canadian Government contain the clause that the ship must be built in Canada. We have given notice to the woUd to this effect. We gave the contract for that great icebreaker we are having built for the St. Lawrence to the Canadian Vickers Company, Montreal, who were the lowest tenderers complying with the clause that the vessel must be built in Canada. In regard to the vessels to which my hon. Mend has referred, the Quebec Harbour Commissioners tell me that they were not aware of our policy of having all Government vessels built in Canada at the time they gave those contracts, and they said it would have been impossible for any shipyard in Canada to have delivered the boats in time. That is the statement made by Mr. Price, through the secretary of the board, and I have no doubt it is correct. With regard to the sale of property to which my hon. friend has referred, I might say that as soon as I heard of it I at once brought it to the attention of the chairman of the Quebec Harbour Commission. Mr.' Price tells me that he is satisfied that Mr. Gravel, who has, I believe, an admirable reputation in Quebec, and is one of its leading business men, had no knowledge whatever of the transaction; that, so far as he was concerned, there was no wrong-doing at all, and that he did not in any way convey the information which led to the persons speculating in and making a profit out of this land. The matter has not come up for the first time now. It was first brought to my attention in a newspaper article, .and I at once communicated with Mr. Price, who said that he was satisfied that there was no wrong-doing on the part of Mr. Gravel.

Does not my hon. friend think it .strange that a property bought on the 29th March, 1913, for $2,000 should be sold four days afterwards to the Harbour Commission for $4,500? Does not my hon. friend think that that increase is rather questionable?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

I admit it was a pretty
