On motion of Hon. J. D. Reid (acting Minister of Railways and Canals), the House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolution, Mr. Blondin in the chair:
IMr. Lemieux.]
Resolved, that It is expedient to provide for the cost of building three railway bridges in the province of New Brunswick, one across the St. John river at or near Andover, in the county of Victoria; one across the St. John river at or near Mistake, in the county of Kings; and one across the Kennebecasis river, at or near Perry Point, in the said county of Kings.

In the year 1912 the Dominion Parliament passed an Act by which they agreed to guarantee the bonds on the bridges mentioned in this resolution in connection with the St. John Valley Railway Company in New Brunswick. The railway company and the province of New Brunswick have found on further investigation that the railway company will not be able to build the bridges for the amount originally estimated by them. They are unable to proceed with the construction of the bridges without further assistance from the Dominion Government. As it is the intention of the Government to take this railway over and operate it in connection with the Intercolonial railway when it is completed, the Government have decided to give further aid towards the bridges mentioned. However, instead of guaranteeing the bonds, as was originally done in the Act of 1912, the Government have come to the conclusion that it would be much better for them to build the bridges themselves. They will call for tenders and let the contract and the work will be carried to completion through the Department of Railways and Canals. When the bridges are completed, they will be owned entirely by the Dominion, Government. In the former agreement the Dominion Government agreed to allow the railway company to use all the bridges for fifteen years without interest, and after that the provincial Government was to get a certain percentage of the earnings on the St. John Valley railway, and the St. John Valley Railway Company were to get any profit there might be over and above the earnings and the payment of the interest on the bonds that will be issued against the bridges in connection with this railway. In this Bill it is proposed that the bridges, including all necessary approaches, will be built by the Dominion Government and that they shall belong to and be the property of His Majesty. After the bridges are completed the Minister of Railways may enter into an agreement with the Government of the province of New Brunswick and the St. John and Quebec Railway Company, under which agreement it will be

provided that for the fifteen years after the bridges are completed no charge shall be made in respect to the cost of construction of the bridges. In other words, the original arrangement of allowing the bridges to be used for fifteen years free of interest will be carried out, but after the fifteen years His Majesty shall be entitled to the gross earnings of the bridges; being such proportion of the said gross earnings of the railway, exclusive of the railway and of the bridges, a3 the cost of the bridges bear to the combined cost of the railway and of the bridges. The earnings of the bridges in proportion to the total cost of the railway will be paid to the Dominion Government.

I am happy to say that the minister and myself are very nearly in agreement over this Bill, and I congratulate the minister and the Government on the course they have taken in absolutely eliminating the St. John and Quebec Railway Company from having anything whatever to do, either directly or indirectly, with the construction of these bridges. I only wish it were possible to go to the same extent in the province of New Brunswick, that my hon. friend the minister is going in so far as the federal Government is concerned. I do not like to say to him, that I told him to do this, but I want to say to the people of this country that in the speech I delivered here three or four weeks ago I advised him to do it, in view of the great scandal that is going on in the province of New Brunswick at present.
He put it in the Bill on account of what you said.
I will not go to the extent of saying that, and I give the minister credit for wanting to do what is. right.

Do not give him too
much credit.
You will spoil him.

I pointed out that things were not going on properly in our province in respect to this railway question and I say so now, but if the minister carries out the proposals in the Bill-an advance copy of which he was good enough to send me a few moments ago-I am satisfied that so far as the bridges are concerned the thing will be carried out fairly and honestly. I know the minister will carry it out according to his promise, and that he will call for public tenders, and I believe there will be no boodling so far as that part of the transaction is Concerned. I have not had time to examine the details of the Bill, but they will come up for discussion later. The Bill, of course, is not yet before the House, but I call the attention of the minister to that clause in it with reference to the proclamation which would mean that the construction of these bridges might be postponed for a year.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The Government could proclaim it at any time.

They cannot proclaim
this Act until after legislation is passed in New Brunswick and that might be a year hence.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Would it not be sufficient, if there was an Order in Council passed by the provincial Government agreeing to bring in legislation at the next session? There would have to be legislation by the province, and of course my hon. friend sees the difficulty there.

We want this work finished as quickly as possible, so that we may be able to forget this thing altogether. We want these bridges built now. When the Bill comes to its second reading, possibly some arrangement can be made with respect to that. I am satisfied that the Minister has worked out this scheme properly. The original scheme was that the Government was to guarantee the bonds to the extent of one million dollars, upon which the federal Government was to pay the interest for fifteen years; now the federal Government owns the bridges, and the same idqp will be carried out by charging no rental to the railway company for fifteen years. After the fifteen years the Government will charge the railway company along the same lines as those in the original agreement. I think the minister has his Bill properly drawn along these lines, and I therefore have great pleasure in congratulating the minister and stating that he has my hearty approval for this resolution, subject of course to the necessary amendment to which I have called attention.

I congratulate the acting Minister of Railways, and I am sure he is filling well the position of the Minister of Railways during his absence, in so far as these bridges are concerned. I am glad to see by this Bill that the building of three bridges means that one bridge will be built over the St. John river at Andover, in my constituency, which means that the

railway will be built as far as Grand Falls. Last year we endeavoured to get a subsidy from this Government to build the railway from Andover to Grand Falls, but the Minister of Railways refused, telling us that it was not advisable to build a railway parallel to the Canadian Pacific railway for that distance. The fact that they are going to build a bridge across the St. John river at Andover means that the St. John Railway Company will run on the other side of the river, and it will not necessarily parallel the Canadian Pacific railway. Like the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) I believe in the good will of the acting Minister of Railways. I hope he will endeavour to see that these bridges will be constructed as soon as possible, and if the Bill is not what it should be with regard to the proclamation, we have his assurance that nothing will be allowed to interfere with the speedy construction of these bridges. I hope that will be the case.
The Bill has been prepared with that very object in view, and it shows very plainly that our intention is to carry out this work.

Is this not a new departure? Is there a precedent for action of this kind ? The Government propose to build and own bridges on a line of railway which is under different ownership, and on which they will own nothing except the bridges. If there is precedent for this in Canadian railway building, I am not aware of it.

I do not know if the hon. member is aware that it is the intention of the Government that* the Intercolonial railway should operate the St. John Valley road-that is, this road when completed will be really a. part of the Intercolonial Railway system. The original arrangement was that a bridge company was to be formed to build these bridges, which were then to be leased to the railway, and we were to guarantee the bonds. But it has been decided that we should build the bridges on this line, which as I say, will be part of the Intercolonial railway, so far as operation is concerned.
But I understand that no part of this railway becomes a part of the Intercolonial railway.
Under lease.

By agreement between the company and the Government on a percentage basis, the Intercolonial Railway system is to operate this road. That is all.

Now, it strikes me as peculiar, and a very radical departure, for the Government to build expensive bridges upon a road which they do not own. Certainly, these bridges will be a white elephant on their hands if the road should prove unsuccessful. I cannot understand why the bridges could not be built under an agreement similar to that made with regard to the rest of the road. There may be good reasons for it, but I do not know what they are. If the building of these bridges means the difference between New Brunswick having this road and not having it, I should be glad to see the Government assist in building the bridges. But I think it must appear to the acting Minister of Railways himself that it is an anomaly to have a railway partly owned by the Government and partly owned by others.
I must say also to the Prime Minister (Mr. Borden) that while he is dealing with - a lavish hand with the province of New Brunswick so far as railways are concerned, he is, I fear, neglecting his own province.
The province of New Brunswick 5 p.m. has advantages in railway facilities which the province of Nova Scotia never had. The further you go east, the further you go out on what has been called the ' Long Wharf ' of the Dominion, the province of Nova Scotia, the further you go from the railway centre. The province of New Brunswick is crossed and recrossed by lines of railways. In Quebec they have very great advantages in the extent of their railway facilities; and, when you come to Ontario, you find that from east to west, it is gridironed with railways. When the Prime Minister proposes that this extraordinary course should be adopted to give further railway facilities to a province that is already well served, he should not forget his own native province. He must not forget that we have no other representative in the Cabinet but himself, nobody else to whom we can go about such matters. I know that his attention is burdened with great questions of many kinds, but his native province looks to him and expects him to see that its railway interests are not neglected. He is making a new step in the history of railway building under this measure. And while he is assenting to dispositions of this kind for railway development in one part of the country, I hope that the railway projects of his own province, which we have been putting before the House and before himself, will receive serious consideration at his hands.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I shall bear in mind the suggestion of my hon. friend and shall endeavour to see to it that the interests of my own province are not neglected. As to this particular case, we had undertaken to guarantee the bonds for $1,000,000. It turned out that nearer $3,000,000 was required. We had' the choice of one of three courses:	First, to do nothing; second, to
increase the guarantee of bonds to $3,000,000 or thereabouts, and, third, to build the bridges ourselves. Upon consideration of the whole question, a question that was not without difficulties, we concluded that the last-named course was the best. And while I am mindful of the claims that my own province has upon me, I can hardly refrain from what seems reasonable in this case, merely for the reason that I did not happen to be born in the province of New Brunswick.
Will the acting minister tell us if he has estimates of what these bridges will cost?
I am informed that they will cost less than $3,000,000; I think the estimate is something like $2,800,000; but we ask for $3,000,000.

Was that an estimate
made by an engineer?

Yes, the estimate was made by Mr. Montserrat, chairman of the Quebec Bridge Commission, who is supposed to be one of the best bridge engineers in Canada. He made a careful investigation and a report with an estimate of the cost.

Do I understand that
we have the promise of the minister that these bridges will be built by contract after public tender?
By tender, with public competition.	.

I am glad to hear that. For fear of agreeing with the minister to too great an extent to suit some of my hon. friends around me, I wish to say that' I cannot agree with him in the statement he made some time ago that they found the million-dollar guarantee not sufficient to build these bridges.
I wish to congratulate my hon. friend upon this. I think the Prime Minister put it very fairly when he said that three courses were open: the first was that of doing nothing; the second was that of carrying out the bond guarantee or increasing it, and the third was that of building the
bridges themselves. I think that they ha.e done just what they ought to have done. I want to tell the committee that it was not necessary to increase the bond guarantee, and it was not necessary to change this legislation one iota, because if the money which had been voted by the province of New Brunswick had been honestly accounted for, there would have been enough money to have built the road. However, I congratulate my friends for taking the next best step with a view to creating some sort of order out of chaos.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I cannot allow my hon. friend to make the assertion which he has made before this committee without saying that h>
has no justification or warrant for making it. Certain charges have been made in connection with the Valley railway and the party who made that charge in the legislature of New Brunswick asked that a committee be appointed to investigate the matter. The legislature, composed almost entirely of supporters of the present local Government, amended the resolution and provided that a commission should be appointed to investigate these charges. A commission was named consisting of Sir Frederick Barker, ex-chief justice of the Supreme Court of the province of New Brunswick, Hon. H. A. McKeown, judge of the Supreme Court and Mr. W. S. Fisher, a leading merchant of the city of St. John. Unfortunately, owing to the state of his health, Sir Frederick Barker declined to act, although he expressed his entire willingness to do so when approached on the subject before the commission was appointed. Another commissioner is to be appointed to take Sir Frederick Barker's place; I understood that he was to be appointed this week. Who he is, I do not know. That commission is to inquire into these charges and I think that until these charges are inquired into and until	the evidence	is brought
before the commission my hon. friend is not warranted in making the assertion that he has made before this committee. This whole matter, therefore, is now under consideration and will be inquired into by this independent commission composed of gentlemen in no sense partisan; gentlemen on one side or the other of politics, who have the confidence of the people of New Brunswick. In view Oif these circumstances, I do not think that my hon. friend ought to make such assertions as he has .made and I do not feel that I ought to allow 'them to go unchallenged. With regard to the cost of the bridges, I

may say that the estimate made by Mr. Montserrat for the bridge crossing the St. John river is about $2,063,000. The bridge is expensive because of the great difficulty experienced in getting satisfactory foundations, Mr. Montserrat, after having inspected the different sites along the river, has made the estimate which I have mentioned. It is estimated I believe, that the crossing of the Kennebecasis river will cost something in the neighbourhood of $500,000. These are the facts and figures as I have them; I have seen Mr. Montserrat's report and I can speak (with absolute accuracy as to his estimate of the cost of the bridge. Probably $3,000,000 will be more than enough to cover the cost of all these bridges.

I appreciate the little
lecture which my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries has given me, but I do not know that it was entirely unexpected, because this is a rather sore point with my hon. friend. I do not wonder that he objects to having these skeletons dragged out into the open, but the skeletons are there just the same. It is all very well for my hon. friend to .say that the committee of the legislature, because it was practically all on one side, did not think it fair to investigate the thing. Let me tell my hon. friend that the gentleman who took the responsibility oif making these charges wanted to have them investigated by that very same unfair tribunal. It is rather a remarkable thing that when the man who made the charges wanted them investigated by that tribunal, that tribunal (was not willing to grant the investigation. It is another remarkable thing that six weeks after the charges were made no other tribunal has been appointed far purposes of investigation. I do not intend to quarrel with my hon. friend about this matter here; we may quarrel about it elsewhere, but I do want to tell him that he cannot find another instance where a man having laid certain charges against members of a provincial Government, after a lapse of six weeks there are still no signs of the charges being investigated.

I thought that there was some prospect of the dawn of a millenium so far as the hon. member for C'arleton is concerned because of his having approved anything done by this Government, but that prospect is as far away as ever. The hon. member could not possibly voice his approval without putting in what might be

called a joker; without dragging in some extraneous matter that has absolutely nothing to do with what is before the House, but which is introduced simply to display to the committee the fact that the hon. gentleman still retains all that virulence of feeling .and violence of language that is so characteristic of him. My hon. friend seems to experience some suspicion because the legislature of. the province of New Brunswick saw fit, instead of appointing a. committee of the House to investigate the charges that have been made against the provincial Government by a member of the legislature, to appoint a Royal Commission. They appointed upon that Royal Commission men, one of whom at least was not of their own political faith. My horn, friend cannot understand, it seems, that men in political life may be actuated by a spirit of absolute fairness to an opponent and so he attempts to cast some suspicion upon that commission, because there are upon it two judges of the Supreme Cburt of the province of New Brunswick, one a retired chief justice, Sir Frederick Barker, a man who stands high in the estimation not only of the people of the province which has been honoured by his services but by the whole of Canada; a man who is known from the Atlantic to the Pacific.

I understand that he
has refused to act.

I am speaking now of the men who were appointed, as showing the desire for absolute fairness on the part of the legislature of New Brunswick, so that there should he no -abuse cast upon them by reason of the fact that practically all the members of the legislature of the province are of one political stripe. But my hon. friend would not he very glad if a committee of the House had been appointed, all of whom would not be Conservatives, and if their findings were adverse to the side which he represents. My hon. friend, in this House and everywhere else would say that it was a packed committee. He knows-and .hence his bitterness-that that excuse is taken from him because of the fact that the gentlemen who have been appointed on that commission are men of high standing, men absolutely removed from politics, men whose findings will be received by this country as based upon absolute facts and fully justified. Is that what is the matter with my hon.

friend, and is that why he could not even allow this harmless Bill, which he admits is in the best interests of the country, to pass without sneering at the Legislature and the Government of New Brunswick?

Fortunately, the somewhat violent exhibition of temper on the part of the hon. member for Kings (Mr. Fowler) will not defeat this legislation. I am very glad indeed for that. I have been dressed down by the hon. member three or four times during this session, and I am still living. I am not sure that this thing can go on forever without something being said in return. I wish to tell my hon. friend that I do not often have suspicions that I do not voice, and my friend knows too much about what has taken place in New Brunswick in the last six or eight weeks to talk very much in this House. There is no necessity for him and me quarreling over what has taken place down there in the past, we will have something to say about that in the future. I agree with him in one thing, and that is the complete suitability of Sir Frederick Barker to act as commissioner. I am somewhat surprised that he should have been appointed one evening at eight o'clock and that he should have declined the next day to act. It may be that there was a good excuse. It may be that the Government believed that Sir Frederick Barker would act, and had he been able to act no one would have been better pleased than I. It may surprise the hon. member for Kings, when he talks about my not having the ability to appreciate a fair man, that I was the first person to name Sir Frederick Barker to the Government. I stated before it was decided to appoint a Royal Commission, that if a commission were appointed I would be willing to accept Sir Frederick Barker as sole commissioner. There is no gentleman in Canada for whom I have a higher regard than for Sir Frederick Barker, and there is not a man in New Brunswick, liberal or Conservative, who does not feel great regret that that gentleman has not been able to act upon the commission. I know there was not a newspaper in New Brunswick that did not approve in the heartiest manner of the personnel of the commission. The fault I find with the Government of New Brunswick is the delay in filling up the breach. Surely they should be able to get some man in New Brunswick to take Sir Frederick Barker's place, because it is now nine or ten days since he 245
was appointed. I think that is too long to wait in the case of an important matter like this.

I do not think my hon. friend is entitled to claim credit for suggesting the appointment of Sir Frederick Barker, as, when the appointment of a royal commission was first suggested, practically everybody suggested Sir Frederick Barker for that position. My hon. friend must share the credit with a great many people in New Brunswick. If Sir Frederick Barker does not act, it is simply because the condition of his health prevents him. The position may be filled by a judge who also holds the full respect of the people of New Brunswick. I do not know of any judge on the Bench who does not hold that respect, but I am sure that the gentleman who will take the place of Sir Frederick Barker, who is unable to act, will be just as well deserving of respect as Judge Barker himself.

That might be quite a
contract. However, that is all that we want.

That is quite a contract, but I think there are also other judges who hold the respect of the people of New Brunswick, and that this commission will be one with which no one can find fault. As far as any disclosures that are to be made, of which my hon. friend speaks, I am always glad to have these things come out if there are any things to come out. There is nothing that can affect myself in Tegard to the matter and I expect to meet my hon. friend at the investigation, where we will be able to thresh out a whole lot of things.
Will the minister say if he has consulted the general manager of the Intercolonial in Tegard to the structures to be built under this Bill?
No, I have not.

I wished to know that as we have had the doctrine laid down by Mr. Gutelius that we ought to have wooden trestles on roads of this construction, that it is a mistaken policy to erect steel bridges on a road such as we are building in New Brunswick. I am surprised that my hon. friend did not draw that matter to the attention of the general manager and have his advice, as this road was to be erected by the Intercolonial. I have no doubt he would be very much opposed to the expense of erecting steel bridges on a road of this character, in New Brunswick or anywhere



else. The minister should explain why he has adopted steel in place of wood in this case.
I am acting on the report of the engineer who was sent down to look into the matter, Mr. Montserrat.

Is it the intention, in the construction of these bridges, to have provision on them for highway traffic? If so, will the Dominion Government supply that, or will it be provided by the provincial government? I am not particularly interested in these bridges, but in the West we find that there has been a great waste of public resources in building railroad bridges across large rivers when a small additional expenditure would have provided traffic facilities and furnished a tremendous advantage to the people of the locality. I quite appreciate that it is not the business of the railway company or of the Dominion Government to do that, but there would be such a tremendous advantage and economy in using the main structure of the railroad bridge for the carrying of the roadway that I would think it would be sound policy, wherever such a bridge is being constructed within the knowledge or on the responsibility or in any way under the aid of the Dominion Government, that the government of the province in which the bridge is situated should be approached with the offer that they would have the privilege of making arrangements for the adding of traffic facilities on fair terms.
I do not urge that the Dominion Government is responsible for this matter, but it has a general interest in everything that concerns the welfare of the people of this country, and I would suggest as a matter of policy in the public interest that when such cases arise, particularly in the West, the provincial authorities be given an opportunity of making some such arrangement.

Of course an agreement will foe made between the province of New Brunswick, this Government, and the railway company in connection, with the building of these bridges. I think the point taken by my hon. friend is a good one. I understand him to mean that provision should be made for traffic teams alongside the railway. I would be glad to direct the attention of the Minister of Railways and Canals to my hon. friend's suggestion, and if it is at all feasible in this particular instance I have no doubt the minister will carry it out.

I am not particularly interested in this case. I just wish to bring
[Mr. Sinclair.!
the idea to the public mind with a view to instances that might arise later on in the western provinces.
Resolution reported and concurred in.
Mr. REID thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 201) to amend the St. John and Quebec Railway Company Act.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.
On motion of Hon. C. J. Doherty (Minister of Justice), Bill no. 190, to amend the Judges Act was read the second time and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Blondin in the Chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It has been suggested
to me that a difficulty has arisen in the Maritime Provinces under the provisions of the present Judges Act. What is complained of is that certain judges who do not reside in the county town-and they aTe not bound by law to reside in the county town-are, under the present Act, precluded from receiving the travelling allowance for holding court in a county town, and also precluded from receiving the travelling allowance when they hold court in the town in which they reside. It has been represented that there are two or three cases where the judge resides in a town other than the county town, but in which the business to be dealt with is as large as, or possibly larger than, the business to be dealt with in the county town. Those being the facts, the result is that that judge has to go to the county town to do his work and gets no travelling allowance; while he is also exempting the country from paying him any travelling allowance when he does the work in the town in which he has chosen to reside. I quite realize that under those circumstances the country is getting an unfair advantage because of the fact that the judge does not reside in the county town. Of course, if he were bound by law to reside in the county town, there would be nothing more to be said, but he is not. I think that is a situation that in fairness to the judge ought to be met, and to meet it I am proposing, and I move now, to amend the present Bill by adding as section 5, the following:
5. Subsection (c) of section 18 of the principal Act is repealed, and the following substituted therefor:
(c) No judge of a county court shall receive any travelling allowance for courts or chambers held at the county town of the county or union of counties wherein he resides-provided,

however, that this subsection shall not apply to any such judge residing at a town (other than the county town) at which the volume of court or chamber work done is established to the satisfacttion of the Minister of Justice to he as great or greater than that done at the county town.

Inasmuch as I happen to be the person who brought this matter to the attention of the Minister of Justice, I thank him for the consideration that he has given to it. While his amendment to some extent meets the objection that I raised against the existing provisions, I think it throws on the Minister of Justice a certain amount of responsibility, and perhaps attention, that he ought to be relieved of. I think that if his amendment were to the effect that where the town in which the judge resides is larger in point of population than the county town, it would fairly meet the objection that has been raised. Where the population is larger the presumption is, of course, there is more legal business to be done, and I would suggest that he accept the change in the amendment that I have proposed.

I think it would be preferable to specify the particular cases instead of making the application general, because it might open the door to judges living elsewhere than in the county towns. Conditions in the Maritime provinces are a little different from those of Ontario. I understand that a judge in the Maritime provinces has to look after two or three counties, whereas in Ontario there is only one county town for each district. I think that if the law is made general it will militate against the county town.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Under the provision I have suggested the judge would have no pecuniary object in living in any other town than the county town, because this amendment would only apply to him if he selected a town where there was at least as much judicial work to do as in the county town itself. He would be giving at least as much of his time without any travelling allowance charged to the country as he would be if he lived in the county town. He would not in any way benefit if he lived elsewhere than in the county town. Whether there are other temptations to take judges away from county towns I do not know. Of course, this would not affect any judge in any province where his residence is fixed by law. He will have to live where the law tells him to live. But I understand that in the Maritime provinces the present 245i
law does not determine where the judge must reside, and I understand there are actually existing cases where a judge lives-in some other place than the county town-where the business is greater than it is-in the county town. I am told that the judge of the county in which Campbellton is situated resides in Campbellton, that some other place is the county town, and that the business done at Campbellton is as large, or larger, than that in the county town. If these facts are correct, then the judge is being unfairly treated. I think the same thing happens in regard to Dorchester, and also in New Glasgow and Pictou. My hon. friend from Kings tells me that the same thing happens in his county. We ought to make provision to meet every case wherever it arises. I cannot, nor can the members of the House, verify the cases in which it happens. The suggested amendment will entitle a judge to his allowance at the county town wherever he satisfies the department that there is no loss to the country by reason of his residing elsewhere than at the county town because there is as much work at the town he resides in as at the county town. I think that in the province of Ontario the residence of judges is fixed by statute, so that this legislation would not affect the judges of that province in any case.

The residence of the judge is fixed by the Ontario statute in the-county for which he is appointed, and under the Judges' Act he is not entitled to any travelling allowance if he takes up another place of residence than the county town.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That is the way it
stands at present. A judge is not allowed anything at all if he does not live at the county town. If he chooses to go and live elsewhere he forfeits any allowance for work done in the other place that he has gone to. When he chooses to live elsewhere no doubt the country escapes paying him an allowance if he works in either one of the two places. If he chooses to live in the county town, he has his allowance if he goes elsewhere. If he chooses not to live in the county town, he forfeits his allowance in the place where he resides and also in the county town. That is the penalty of his not living in the county town. Where the fact is that at his place-of residence he is called upon to devote just as much of his time to judicial work as he would be in the county town, the

country suffers in no way if he is paid his allowance when he is at the county town. The country is put in the same position as if he had lived in the county town. I understand that in the particular cases that are referred to, the places where the judges do actually live, are now, whatever they may have been in the past, more important centres than the county towns actually are.

I do not dispute that but I am afraid that if you make the law general it will induce judges in other counties to reside elsewhere than in the county town and we do not want to encourage them to do that. I think that we should encourage them to live in the county town where most of the business is done. When judges sit in chambers they leave the papers to be filed with the clerk of the court. It is much more convenient to do legal business in the county town than in "other places.

I think the proposition submitted by my hon. friend, from Richmond (Mr. Kyte) solves the difficulty that the minister wants to overcome. In a great many cases it would be almost impossible to ascertain the amount of work that is done in one town as compared with another. But speaking for the situation in the Maritime provinces, and particularly for my own county, I think the criterion of population is one which ought to satisfy the department and one which is eminently fair.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The population could
not be regarded as a very good indication of the time that a judge has to spend in holding court. If we allowed the judge to go away from the county town to a place where there might be very little judicial business, when there was a great deal to do in the county town, it might result in the country having to pay a great deal more for allowance than if he lived in the county town. I am willing to meet the judges if I can meet them without imposing on the country a larger burden than the country would have to bear if they did live in the county town. Population would be a very unreliable basis to go upon because a great deal of business will have to be done at the county town, because it is the county town, without regard to population. For instance, the criminal business will have to be done there and it is a large item. I feel that in making this suggestion I have gone as far as I can to meet the wish and desire of the judges.
I Mr. Doherty.]

In my own county
the judge lives ten miles away but communication between the two points is very easy. You go to where the judge resides and get an ex parte order, or you have an unopposed motion to make in chambers, the judge initials the order and then you take the order back to the county town and the clerk signs it there. It would be impossible to get any data as to where the greatest amount of business is done; in fact, it is just where the judges happen to sit and where they happen to be when they make the order. The judge may hear a motion in the town in which he resides, he may send his judgment to the county town, the order would be taken out and consented to, perhaps, and would be dated from the county town, and the seal would be affixed there. Naturally, a difficulty would arise under these circumstances. But I do not see where the difficulty could exist if you made population the criterion because more population naturally produces more business. I remember that some time ago an attempt was made in our province to get some data to indicate the relative amount of business in the town for the purpose of making some representations to the Justice Department and the Bar had the greatest possible difficulty in getting that data together. I repeat, I do not see where the difficulty could arise if my hon. friend would make the population the criterion because, prima facie, the more population the more litigation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Unfortunately for that
theory, one of the learned judges who is interested in this legislation, makes his case on the strength of the fact that, not living in the county town, he had to go there a large number of times and get nothing for it. I think it is the very judge that my hon. friend refers to. His letter says that there is more criminal work in his county than in the town he actually lives in. He is able to ascertain that. I think we ought to give a certain amount of credence at least to what a judge represents to us. We pay these bills now on the judge's own certification, or practically we do so, because we have no reason to suspect the Information which a judge gives us. I think I have gone as far as I would be justified in going.

Is it the understanding of the minister that a county court judge residing in a county town is entitled to his travelling expenses if he has to go

to another town in the same county to hold a court?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, under this amendment.
Does the minister say he would not be so entitled now?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Under the section as
it stands the judge gets no allowance for work done in his county town, and no allowance for work done in the town in which he resides.

My question was: If
the judge is residing in the county town now and there is another large town in the county where he holds court, is he entitled to his travelling expenses, under the law as it now stands, if he has to go to that town and hold a court?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

When the legislature of any province imposes a duty upon a county court judge of an important character and creates a county.court judge's court, a particular tribunal, to deal with that matter, and when the judge goes there holding his court under that statute, I should think there should be no question in the world, about his being paid his travelling expenses as a judge of the county court. I have a case in mind where the judge of a county court had to go outside of his county to hold a court, under a statute of our province in connection with a municipal election petition, and I am sorry to say he was not paid, although he sent in his bill. I cannot appreciate where the line is to be drawn. I think he should be paid for work of that kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The legislature of that
province attributed that work to the judges and attributed pay to them for doing it, so that the legislature dealt with it as something quite outside of the functions of the county court. It provided that these gentlemen should do that work and	provided pay for	them for
doing it. I should think that one would have to draw the line between duties attributed to a county court judge which are properly of a judicial nature and duties which may be of a kind that might well have been assigned to any other intelligent person. What the hon. gentleman is discussing is something that does not bear upon any amendment to the law; it is a .matter that would have to be determined in accordance with what would be determined
tc- be a judicial duty. Does the hon. member suggest that if the legislature chooses to say that a county court judge shall do work that has no connection with any judicial proceeding, we should pay his travelling expenses for doing it?

I do not think the
minister will contend that the trial of election contested cases is a matter that could be assigned to any one but a judge or some-' one learned in the law. In the revision of the Nova Scotia statutes a few years ago, the parties who had charge of that revision made the trial of election petitions, in connection with municipal elections, Dominion elections, and provincial elections, precisely the same, so that the man who sits on the Bench to try a question as to a municipal election is adjudicating on exactly the same law as if he were trying a petition against a member of this House. Surely the minister would not think that work of that kind could be entrusted to a layman?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Does not the province
pay for it?

I would like the Prime Minister to pay attention to this because it is a matter affecting his province of Nova Scotia. Before the Judges' Act of 1905 there was a provision in our law that the county court judge should get a standing allowance of two hundred dollars a year for the outside work he did, and for many years there was a petty allowance of two and a half dollars a day for a judge in Nova Scotia when he went to try these election cases. Under the Judges' Act of 1905 the two hundred dollars' allowance was wiped out and a new provision took its place. It so happened that the province of Nova Scotia did not repeal its two and a half dollar a day business when the new Judges' Act came in, and up to the instance I have in mind I think the judges were always allowed travelling expenses when they went outside their own county. I do not know of a single instance, except this one, where the line was drawn. I submit that when a county court judge has to do important work of this kind he should be allowed his travelling expenses. I shall take care to ask the Legislature of Nova Scotia to repeal this tuppeny-hapenny allowance of two and a half dollars a day, if that is all that stands in the way of judges getting their travelling expenses under certain circumstances.

This amendment changes the law in another respect. It says: that

no judge of a county court shall receive travelling expenses for courts or chambers held in the county court or of the union of counties in which he resides, whereas the present law says: where he is obliged by law to reside. The senior judge of my district resides in Ottawa. He would not toe entitled to an allowance for sitting in chambers at Ottawa, but under this amend-[DOT] ment he would be allowed for sitting in chambers in the county town of Prescott and Russell.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If toy law his residence is fixed in Ottawa then that is the place where by law he is bound to reside, and therefore he gets no allowance in Ottawa. The intention of the law was that there should be one place where a judge would not toe entitled to an allowance, namely, the place where the law says he must live in, or, if he lives at some different place then the place in which he actually lives. Where the law prescribes no place of residence the assumption is that he should live at the county town and therefore he gets nothing for services at the county town and nothing at the town he does reside in if he wishes to reside away from the county town. Where the law fixes the place where he does reside, then the section applies to that place and to no other place.
His residence is in Ottawa, but it is not recognized by law.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If it is not, then he has no right to live here.

He has been charging travelling expenses for sitting in Three Rivers and Ottawa. He asked for permission by Order in Council of the Lieutenant Governor to sit in Chambers in Ottawa, and he has been charging travelling allowances for sitting in Ottawd, though he resides here, pretending that he was residing in the county town of Prescott and Russell.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I will look into the facts. If they are as stated, the judge is wrong.

He claims he is right, and I claim he is practising a fraud on the Government.

On section 2-seven commissioners ap-pointable toy Order in Council:

What is the
object of this change? I understood the hon. minister to say on introducing the Bill that it was the intention to increase the number of commissioners from five to seven, but he gave no reason for it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The Government has
thought it desirable that the commission should be enlarged to seven. In the first place, there are, I think, three residing outside the city of Quebec. In addition to that the commission has no member or members who have been appointed by this Government. I have discussed the matter with the chairman, Sir George Garneau, and,he agreed that so far as he was concerned, there should be an increase. We have not interfered with the commission, which, I think, is proper. The commission consists of men of high standing, including Sir
6 p.m. Edmund Walker, Hon. Mr. Taschereau, Hon. Mr. Turgeon, and Mr. Bickerdike. Nevertheless it has appeared to the Government desirable that there should be an increase.

The reason
given by my hon. friend is not much of a reason-simply that the Government desires

to increase the number. He says he has conferred with the chairman on the subject. Has there been any official communication, or has there been only verbal communication, between my hon. friend and the chairman?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There has been no official communication from the commission desiring an increase in the number. But I have discussed the matter with the chairman, and so far as he is concerned, he is agreeable that the number should be increased. And, for the reasons I have given, we are of opinion that the number should be increased.

I am sorry,
but I cannot share that opinion. I cannot see any good reason, even after hearing my hon. friend, why the commission should not be composed as it is composed at present. He admits that the commission is one of high standing, and I do not think he can improve the commission in that respect. Of course, we shall have to submit, but I do not think this is an improvement.

There is this also to be said: the personnel of the commission was made by the late Administration irrespective of politics. Sir Byron Walker is a member of the commission, and I understand Colonel Dennison is on it. And is not Colonel Hendry on this commission also?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He is officially by law.

That shows, as I have
said, that the personnel was made irrespective of politics. But this Bill shows that politics is gaining ground in that commission. I see by the papers of Quebec constantly that the commissioners are approached in the awarding of contracts and expropriation proceedings. But every one who knows the personnel of the commission knows that in such a body there is no patronage question. Of course, there are people who think that if they were appointed members of the commission, it would mean for them the millenium. It is a great pity indeed that the personnel of the commission has to be changed. There is no necessity for it, and the change is only a mark of want of confidence on the part of the Government in the present incumbents.
Section agreed to on division.
On section 3-purchase of lands:

What is the
meaning of this?.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
At present the commission is authorized to purchase land after obtaining the authority of Parliament and after it has funds at its disposal. But it must obtain the consent of the Governor in Council. It has been found in the practical working out of the plans, that there have been delays which have resulted in loss of favourable opportunities to buy. As I have said, the commission is one of high standing in which the Government has full confidence, and we have thought it advisable, at their express request, to change the Act so as to permit them to buy land without obtaining the approval in each particular case of the Governor in Council.
There are two provisos which safeguard the matter: first, they must be authorized by Parliament before purchasing these particular lands, and second, there must have been appropriated and be available for the purpose, the necessary funds. That is to say, Parliament must give authority to purchase the land and Parliament must, have provided the money which must stand at the credit of their capital account for that purpose.

I understood my hon. friend to say that the previous consent of the Governor in Council has been the cause of delay, and that the amendment is to allow the commissioners to make purchases without the previous consent of the Governor in Council.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think there is some error in this section in its reference to sections 10 and 11. I will read section 10 of the original Act for the information of the right hon. gentleman:
No land or removable property shall be purchased or acquired by the commission except with previous authority of Parliament, and no expenditure shall be made by the commission until it has been approved by Parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That has, I think, been changed in subsequent legislation.

The minister says that the law to-day is that no purchase can be made by the commission unless it is authorized by Order in Council. This has caused delay and the delays have caused losses, and, in order to obviate these delays and losses, it is proposed now that the commission shall be authorized to make purchases without the consent of the Governor in Council.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Provided that the lands
purchased are lands whose purchase has been authorized by Parliament and provided, consequently, that money has been appropriated by Parliament and is at the disposal of the commission for the purpose.

At all events, you take away one of the restrictions placed by Parliament upon the commissioners and
I	do not think that that is an improvement.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The section as it is at the present has a reference to sections 10 and
II	of the Acts, which are repealed. Section
10	of the Act consists of a section and a subsection. It seems to me that section 10 alone ought to be repealed, because section
11	is repealed by the terms of this section which says that previous to the commission from time to time making expenditures under this Act they must suibmit detailed estimates to the Finance Minister. I think that the form of this amendment will require to be looked into.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The Bill was drafted by
the assistant deputy minister and Mr. Gisborne, the parliamentary counsel, so that every care has been taken. Speaking only from recollection, I think that there is an amending statute to the section that has been read by the right hon. Prime Minister. With regard to this particular section, which gives the commission permission to purchase without the consent of the Governor in Council, I may say that it was introduced upon the express and repeated^ requests of the commission. However, I am quite content to let the matter stand, because it is important.
Section stands.

speechtext:
The telegram which was received from Edmonton was as follows:
Edmonton, Alberta, May 14, 1914. Premier Borden,
Ottawa, Ont.
The Welfare League consisting of merchants and profession men of Edmonton petitioned the city council as follows:	Therefore this
association respectfully urges upon the council of the city of Edmonton to take up the matter with the Dominion Government with a view to securing legislation. 1. Providing for the establishment of free employment bureaus throughout the Dominion for the purpose of supplying reliable information regarding the demands for labour in any particular locality and to give every man a free and equal opportunity to secure employment and to safeguard those already employed; and, (2) To restrict immigration by holding back from entrance into the country or by discouraging in the country from which they come all who belong to the unskilled labouring class except bona fide agricultural labourers, and, (3) To provide work for the unemployed by utilizing the surplus labour now in the country for the construction of public works. The City Council of Edmonton therefore urge you to use your influence to have the Government by grants of money or by furnishing work assist the western cities to care for the unemployed.
Thos. R. Turnbull,
Civic Relief Officer.
The first suggestion in the telegram, that free employment bureaus should be established for the purpose of supplying reliable information regarding demands for laboui in any particular locality, would, of course, require more consideration than the Government have been able to give to it in

the interim. So far as the question of immigration is concerned, I understand that, not only under this Administration but under the former Administration, the ideal which is set forth in the second clause of the memorial has been followed; there has been no change made in that regard under the present Administration. The third suggestion is that work for the unemployed should be provided, as far as possible, by utilizing surplus labour for the construction of public works. We shall, of course, give that the very best consideration that can be given to it, and such attention as may be possible in the public interest. The reply which I have sent to Mr. Turnbull is as follows:
Ottawa, Ont., May 18, 1914. Thos. R. Turnbull,
Civic Relief Officer,
Edmonton, Alberta.
Telegram received. Your suggestions will received immediate careful consideration of Government. Meantime representations of City Council as to providing work for unemployed have been placed before such departments of Government as employ labour to considerable extent and have been commended to consideration and attention of the ministers of those departments.

I desire to call the attention of the House to a case of com-tempt of the high court of Parliament by the Minister of Customs. On the 16th of March last, an order was passed:
For a copy of all recommendations, protests, petitions, and representations received by the Government or any department or minister thereof, regarding the appointment of the present collector of customs at Antigonish, and of all the letters, telegrams and correspondence relating thereto.

Consideration of the proposed motion of Mr. Borden that the House go into Committee to consider certain resolutions respecting the Canadian Northern railway and the amendment of Mr. Macdonald thereto, resumed from Friday, May 15.

Mr. Speaker, considerable has already been said on these proposed resolutions, and it probably will be difficult to introduce any new matter. However, as I feel somewhat strongly on the question, I believe that I should say something regarding not only the resolution, but as well the amendment of the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald). Last session, when the promoters of the Canadian Northern came to Parliament for a grant of
[Mr. Hazen.3
$15,000,000, they stated that they believed that amount would be sufficient to enable them to complete the line, and the Government so informed the House. I took the liberty at that time of predicting that $15,000,000 would be but as a drop in the bucket to these gentlemen, and that it would be practically worthless to them as a sufficient amount for the completion of the Canadian Northern railway. And, Sir, notwithstanding the statements of the Prime Minister and the gentlemen supporting him, made this session on the introduction of these resolutions, and notwithstanding what has been said by the promoters of this enterprise to the effect that $45,000,000 will be sufficient to enable them to complete the line, I venture to predict, in my humble judgment, that $45,000,000, or the proceeds of the guarantee, will not be more than half sufficient to put this line on the standard of a transcontinental railway, and it will not be more than two years, or three years at the outside, when these gentlemen will be back to Parliament again asking for further aid, and one of the strong arguments they will then make in favour of their request will be that the Government of Canada is a partner with them in this enterprise to the extent of $40,000,000.
I think there should have been a very much more sweeping investigation by the Government than there has been, as to whether or not this $45,000,000 will be sufficient to complete this Canadian Northern Railway system. The Government have really made no investigation into that matter, as they made no investigation during the last year or two into the statement made by -these promoters that $15,000,000 would be sufficient. Last year they accepted the statement of the promoters, and this year they have accepted their statement and have come to Parliament saying that $45,000,000 will be sufficient. I have heard gentlemen, who are railway men and who know the condition of the Canadian Northern lines of railway, say that this amount of money will not be more than half, if half, enough to complete these1 lines to the standard of a transcontinental railway, and I have no doubt that such is the case. This summer there should be a thorough investigation to discover whether or not this is the last call of these promoters. I submit that as one strong reason ivhy the amendment of the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) should prevail in regard to these resolutions.

The hon, member for ISouth Ontario (Mr. Smith), in his speech on Friday afternoon, stated that the amendment moved by the hon. member for Pictou, indicated that there was a difference of opinion on this side of the House. A similar statement has appeared in the Ottawa Citizen. If hon. gentlemen opposite are taking any consolation to themselves from the supposition that there is a difference of opinion on this side of the House with regard to these resolutions, they had jbetter disabuse their minds of that at once, because there is absolutely no difference of opinion on this side of the House with regard to what should be done with these resolutions. My right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition stated that we were in favour of coming to the aid of this great enterprise and that it should not be allowed to fail; the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) took practically the same position; but there is no difference of opinion on this side of the House that before any *aid is given there should be a thorough investigation into the whole undertaking and positive knowledge on the part of the Government that this aid not only is required but, when granted, will be sufficient to complete the line. I believe that that same opinion prevails throughout the country. So far as I have been able to ascertain, in going about the country, there appears to be very little difference of opinion in regard to the matter. I believe that the people, with great unanimity, are of the opinion that the stand taken by the Opposition in regard to these resolutions is the correct one, and that this money should not be voted without a full and searching investigation, and that, if it is voted, the Government should have a greater security than they are taking by these resolutions.
I feel that the people of Canada are getting tired of this continual bleeding of the finances of Canada for the exploitation of railway charters. Canada has invested enormous sums of money and has given heavy guarantees in aid of railways; and the people, I believe, are of the opinion that no further aid should be given to this undertaking until it is decided by the most thorough investigation that such aid is necessary, and that the moneys heretofore granted by the Parliament of Canada and by the provincial legislatures have all been devoted exclusively to the construction of this road, and that none of them
have gone into holes and corners where they should not have gone. I have no quarrel with Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann, nor with the enterprise. They have been energetic Canadians, and they have entered upon the building up of an enormous system of railways. I, for myself, am perfectly willing to aid them in a proper manner, as I have by my vote in this House assisted to aid them in the past. But I do not think that these gentlemen should object if they are seriously and strongly criticised in this House. They have received enormous subventions; they have received great aid from the Parliament of Canada, and that money has been spent by them without any supervision on the part of the Parliament or the Government of Canada. There is a strong feeling throughout the country, true or untrue- for myself, I believe it is very largely true [DOT]-that these men, notwithstanding the statement of the Prime Minister that they have made no profits out of the construction of these railways, have made enormous sums of money, not perhaps out of the construction of these railways as out of their dealings with them.
I do not know that it is necessary to say anything very harsh about the resolutions, as it.is not necessary to say anything harsh about Mackenzie and Mann. The resolutions in themselves are bad enough, even clothed with the bright colours painted by the right hon. the Prime Minister, without our casting any reflections upon them. In my opinion, the conduct of Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann in regard to this undertaking should be fully investigated and thoroughly understood.
One objection raised by the right hon. the leader of the Opposition was that, by reason of the agreement entered into between the British Columbia Government and the Canadian Northern Pacific management, this transcontinental railway would be tied up in such a way as to be detrimental. to the people of Canada. The Solicitor General rather impugned that proposition, saying that section 6 of the Railway Act was sufficient in scope to override that agreement and to give the Parliament of Canada exclusive jurisdiction, irrespective of the agreement. Section 6 says:
Where any railway, the construction or operation of which is authorized by a Special Act passed by the legislature of any province, is declared, by any Act of the Parliament of Canada, to be a work for the general advantage of Canada, this Act shall apply to such railway, and to the company constructing or operating the same, to the exclusion of such

of the provisions of the said Special Act as are inconsistent with this Act, and in lieu of any general railway Act of the province.
That is, the Special Act of Incorporation. Section 6 does not say: to the exclusion of any special agreement that may have been entered into between the British Columbia Government and the particular railway. Therefore, as a matter of law, this Parliament has no jurisdiction to deprive the people of the province of British Columbia of any rights which they have under the agreement entered into between them and the Canadian Northern Pacific railway. It would be absolutely ultra vires of this Parliament to pass legislation which they might consider might affect that agreement. It is absolutely impossible for legislation to be passed in this Parliament which will prevent the operation of that agreement, whatever its operation may be.
The agreement is there, made between a railway incorporated by the province of British Columbia and the British Columbia Government and ratified by the legislature of that province, and under these resolutions nothing can deprive the British Columbia Government of the advantages which they have under that 'agreement, whatever those advantages may be. I submit that before the Bill to be based upon these resolutions becomes law, the province of British Columbia should consent to the withdrawal of their agreement with the Canadian Northern Pacific railway or that some means should be taken, either by testing the matter in court or otherwise, to ascertain definitely what are the rights of this Parliament in regard to the matter. Surely the Government of Canada should not become a partner in a railway concern a portion of which railway is under the control or supervision of one of the provinces of Canada. If we are to have a transcontinental railway in which the Government is to be a shareholder, that transcontinental railway should be exclusively and in every particular under the jurisdiction of the Parliament of Canada and under that jurisdiction only; no part of it should be in any particular under the jurisdiction of a provincial government or a provincial legislature. For that reason I say that further consideration of these resolutions should be postponed until the matter is fully and finally settled.

He recognized the fact that, had these men not taken up these charters and had they not secured from practically every province in the Dominion guarantees for their bonds in order that they might sell the securities in the markets
of the world, we would not have had today this great undertaking with its 10,000 miles of railway spread throughout our fair land, covering the best possible territory. If you go through the Northwest territories, you will find that this railway runs through the very best agricultural sections of those western plains. The railway from Edmonton to Vancouver is built by the very best possible route; it is 200 miles shorter than the Grand Trunk Pacific railway, and its grades are better than the grades of any other road on this continent from the prairie to the Pacific ocean. Therefore, we may feel proud and glad to know that we have such men as have undertaken such an enterprise as the Canadian Northern Railway system.
My hon. friend has apparently no fault to find with the manner in which the resolutions have been framed, and he admits that the assistance is necessary. He asks, however, whether this amount will complete the road or not. The hon. gentleman knows full well, if he will read the resolutions, that it is represented to the Government that this amount will be sufficient to complete the road. In addition to that, the resolutions show clearly that the money which is going to be paid for the completion of the road will be paid out on the advice of the Minister of Finance, and that not a dollar of it will be paid out until his agents have satisfied him that, as far as that money is concerned, it has been earned by this corporation.

This goes to show that the various provinces have a very great responsibility in connection with this matter. The prosperity of the settlers along the right of way has been greatly brought, about by the extension of the Canadian Northern Railway system in the various provinces. The hon. member for Welland said this morning that the Canadian Northern had now sufficient money to complete the road, and that there was no reason why further aid should be granted. The hon. gentleman is well aware though that with the aid granled by this resolution the total cost of the road will not exceed $40,000 a mile. The express, telegraph and telephone companies, the and and terminal companies are in excess. If the Canadian Northern had been built through country such as the Grand Trunk Pacific runs the cost would have been much less. The cost of a large portion of the Grand Trunk Pacific is $102,000 a mile, and yet the hon. member for Welland would have it that these men should complete the road for $40,000 a mile.
Is my hon. friend sure about the $102,000 a mile? Those are the biggest figures I have heard yet.
Without a doubt. The statement has been made time and again, and never refuted. The road from Winnipeg to Moncton cost $102,000 a mile.
This is the first time I ever heard that figure.

adian Pacific railway. Ask yourselves the question whether the 'Canadian Pacific railway would have developed the country to a greater extent than it has. The Canadian Pacific railway has developed it along a different line but I do not believe that had the Canadian Pacific railway been left to itself in that great country it would have developed as rapidly as it has during the past few years.
If you drive the 'Canadian Northern into the hands of receivers you retard the development of Canada for a generation. The Government were not responsible for the conditions brought about by the Canadian Northern. The old Government-I do not seriously blame them-assisted that road in order to enable it to bring the products of the West to the Bast. The Canadian Northern with their 5,000 miles of road on the western plains, were compelled to get, if possible, to the eastern provinces in. order that they might be able to carry the manufactured products of the East to the great West for distribution. The building of the Grand Trunk Pacific compelled them, in order to protect their interest, to build the line between Winnipeg and the East, and I do criticise the action of hon. members opposite who will now try to retard the completion of this line to the East.
Where could Mackenzie and Mann have gone to obtain money at the present time? -only to the Dominion Government. Their credit has been exhausted, and the only _ place for them to come was to the Dominion Government. Let me call attention to another fact; not only have towns and cities on the right of way been bnilt up and developed, but industries along the right of way have been materially assisted by the building of this road. Consumers, producers, manufacturers, and others will be materially benefited and will endorse this resolution. The people of England must say that we are doing the right thing in submitting the present resolution to Parliament. By the reduction of the stock from $145,000,000 to $100,000,000 the Board of Railway Commissioners will be in a position to reduce the freight and passenger rates both in the East and in the West, because the general fixed charges on the lines of this railway will amount to two million dollars less than they otherwise would when the road is completed. Another material part of the securities taken by the Government consists of the

steamships belonging to the company, and 1 am informed that the Royal George and the Royal Edward are two of the fastest steamers engaged in the Atlantic service. There are 300 townsites included amongst these securities, as well as the express and telegraph lines belonging to the company. The hon. member for Welland (Mr. German) tried to make us believe that the $12,000,000 of annual fixed charges on this road should be included in the indebtedness of the road to the people of Canada, but he must understand that a large portion of that amount is going to be earned by the road. If he looks at page 14 of the documents brought down, he will find that up to the present the provinces and the Dominion have never been asked to pay one dollar of interest on the guarantees they have given. He will find also that the surplus of the road last year amounted to $1,500,000 and the estimated earnings for 1916 will show a surplus of $1,200,000, and for 1917, $2,400,000, and for 1918 $4,000,000. These are estimated surpluses, it is true, but it is a fact that the road is more likely to be a paying proposition because of the Government coming to its assistance at the present time, than if it were forced into the hands of a receiver. If the hon. gentleman (Mr. German) compares the Canadian Northern and its fixed charges with the Canadian Pacific railway, he must take into consideration that while it is true the fixed charges of the Canadian Pacific railway amount to only about $10,000,000 per annum, they pay ten per cent on $260,000,000 of stock in that road, whereas there is only $100,000,000 of stock in the Canadian Northern. If the time ever comes when the people will be compelled to pay the ten per cent on the $100,000,000 stock, in addition to the $12,000,000 of interest charges, then there will be only $22,000,000 per annum to he paid as compared with the $36,000,000 which is yearly paid by the Canadian Pacific railway. I wish to call attention to the attitude of the premiers of the different provinces with respect to granting aid to the Canadian Northern railway, and it is important that the provinces of this Dominion should realize that they have a very great responsibility in connection with this matter. Viewing the matter, therefore, from this standpoint, It seems to me that if there is any likelihood that the Canadian Northern railway, on account of the magnitude of its through line undertakings may without additional federal assistance, be left In such a position as to compel it to curtail or hold back its branch line development, the loss to western Canada would be very great indeed.
At present we have thousands of settlers who have been patiently waiting for some of these lines for years, and it would be exceedingly unfortunate, under conditions now prevailing, should there be any further delay in providing the branches required.

Most hon. gentlemen opposite who have spoken on this question have urged the early completion of this road, and I ask them how can we better proceed to do that than by supporting the resolution now under discussion. If the amendment presented by the Opposition were carried, it would retard the development of this road, it would create financial panic in Canada, paralyse the system, and injure our credit abroad; whereas if this road is carried to early completion the general prosperity of the country will be increased.
In conclusion, I congratulate the Prime Minister and his Cabinet on the businesslike manner in which they have brought about this splendid arrangement, and I urge on hon. gentlemen opposite that instead of constantly crying blue ruin they should come forward like men and support this resolution. Not a single man of them is able to make a suggestion that would be better in the interests of the country than the proposal now before us. I accuse hon. gentlemen opposite of, during this whole session, crying blue ruin to the detriment of our country. If there are men out of employment in different parts of the country, these hon. gentlemen rush to Parliament to CTy blue ruin. I can only suggest that these hon. gentlemen, who are in the habit of doing this, should join Coxey's army in the country to the south of us. Coxey is marching on to the great city of Washington to-day with some 50,000 followers.
