ment by the Prime Minister and his Cabinet. The Right Hon. R. L. Borden is right on this question, as he has been right on all the great questions that have affected the people of Canada in the past, and I can assure him of my very hearty support on this resolution.

Mr. Speaker, I do not know whether my hon. friend from East Lambton expects me to reply to the latter part of his remarks or not. Perhaps it is not unreasonable to expect him to congratulate the Premier, whom he follows so blindly; and probably he may convince himself that the Premier has made the best trade possible under the circumstances. I do not think, however, it was necessary so severely to castigate the hon. members of the Opposition for preaching blue ruin; but, as this has nothing to do with the matter under discussion, I do not propose elaborating the subject. Perhaps if the hon. members from the western portions of Canada had told the truth about the actual condition of affairs, my hon. friend might have had some cause to complain; but I am afraid conditions have been so bad in that part of the country as to render it necessary to conceal the real facts. I am not going to spend very much time in showing the reasons for the changed condition of affairs in this country in the last three years, but it is most remarkable that, when this Government came into power three years ago, the country was prosperous; the West was booming; the manufacturers of the East were running overtime and on Sundays; the Canadian Northern Company were not begging us for Heaven's sake to save them from blue ruin and bankruptcy; everything was going on in a prosperous, happy condition. Two and a half years of Tory rule in Canada have seen a wonderful transformation in the actual conditions. I say ' have seen ', because I do not want to say that all of this is absolutely due to the bad management of my hon. friends opposite; but I am afraid that, when the history of Canada comes to be written, my hon. friends must be blamed for a great deal of the changed conditions of affairs which have taken place in the last two and a half years.
It is not my intention this afternoon to discuss the general conditions of affairs in Canada. I wish to discuss the condition of Mackenzie and Mann in so far as it relates to the Dominion of Canada; and it seems to me that a discussion of this one

phase of Canadian financial affairs is quite sufficient for any one's attention on one occasion, and that it is not necessary to travel over the whole realm of Canadian financial affairs in order to prove that this Government is in perhaps the worst position in which any Government of Canada has been placed since Confederation. My hon. friend from East Lambton has been very fair in his remarks, as he always is. My hon. friend has done the very best he could to bolster up the position taken by his Premier, and I do not find any fault with him for that. My hon. friend has eulogized the Canadian Northern Railway system, I think, a great deal beyond the actual merits of the case, and has tried to show that no better trade could have been made than the one made by the Government. Again, I would rather expect him to take that course; but notwithstanding all these arguments of my right hon. friend, there are millions of people in Canada who will not be convinced by the arguments put forward by my hon. friend from East Lambton.
There has been a most remarkable absence of authoritative statements from the members of the Government, especially the gentlemen who are really responsible for these proposals. My right hon. friend the Premier gave a general statement of what construction he placed upon the resolutions, and satisfied himself with that. The Solicitor General gave a very learned statement of what he thought were the advantages of the contract, but he spent most of his time in trying to show what a wonderful asset the Canadian Northern railway system was. Since then we have not had a word from any member of the Government. It is a most remarkable thing that about the only speeches we have heard from the Government side of the House since then have been the two wonderful speeches made by my hon. friend the member for Calgary (Mr. Bennett) and my hon. friend the member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle). I watched with a good deal of interest the attitude of the old warhorse of the Conservative party, the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster) during the great speech of the hon. member for Calgary. It was a study; it was worth spending two hours in the House of Commons to see, not to say anything about the wonderful array of facts and arguments presented by the hon. member for Calgary. It was amusing to watch [DOT]the face of my hon. friend the Postmaster General. I have not seen such an unholy

gleam in the eye of that hon. .gentleman since I came to Parliament as I saw when he was listening with such rapture to the arguments put forward by these two hon. members. Any person could see the great amount of gratification in the mind of the Postmaster General at the scathing rebuke which his party was receiving from these two hon. gentlemen, who have been described by the hon. member for Thunder Bay and Rainy River (Mr. Carrick) as the Bull Moose members of the Conservative party.
We have heard nothing from my hon friend the Minister of Finance, although I understand we are to be favoured with a statement from him this afternoon, to which we are all looking forward with the greatest amount of pleasure. My hon. friend assured the House only one short year ago (that iif we gave the Canadian Northern Railway Company a subsidy of $15,000,000 their troubles would all be over, and this great transcontinental system would be completed. That was the substance of his words. The hon. Minister of Finance will attempt to explain those words away; and we shall await with a great deal of interest the manner in which he will explain away the fact that, instead of $15,000,000 settling all the troubles of the Canadian Northern Railway Company and putting them on the highway to prosperity -I am almost afraid to state the amount of money which, in my judgment, from a consideration of the undigested mass of documents which have been thrown to us in the promiscuous manner in which the information asked for has been given to this House, will be necessary to complete the road; but I am safe in saying that $100,000,000 will not do what my hon. friend told us a year ago would be done by the payment of $15,000,000; and the company have already got the $15,000,000. If my hon. friend's arguments and assurances this afternoon have no .more basis of fact than had his arguments and assurances of <ai year ago, I am afraid this House will not pay very much attention to them. Therefore I expect my hon. friend to back up the statements he makes this afternoon by something more than a mere assertion of facts coming from, as I believe, Mackenzie and Mamin, as they came from them last year. I would be the last person to accuse my hon. friend the Minister of Finance of having attempted to mislead this House last year. I have too much respect for my hon. friend to do that. What I do fear is that my hon. friend was
misled by the statements, not so much of Mackenzie and Mann as of a gentleman who has been referred to here a great many times, a gentleman well known to the Minister of Finance; a gentleman very closely associated with him on a memorable occasion in the year 1911; a gentleman who, with my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, led the noble army of martyrs, the eighteen noble patriots who attempted to save Canada to the British Crown and prevent its annexation to the United States; a gentleman who, if common report be true, is responsible for my hon. friend the Minister of Finance occupying the high and exalted position which he occupies in the Government to-day. It is needless to say that I refer to Zebulon A. Lash.

I was referring to Z. A. Lash, something stronger than the Prime Minister. I am afraid that the mis-statements made by his friend Zebulon A. Lash a year ago put my hon. friend the Finance Minister in the position in which he finds himself to-day. I only hope that the information which he will give us on this occasion will come from a better and less interested source than did the information which he received a year ago from Mr. Z. A. Lash.
Another hon. gentleman from whom we have not heard, and who should know something of this matter, is the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen). I think the hon. minister ought to get far enough away from his old friends the Canadian Pacific Railway Company in order to give some reason for the faith which is in him in supporting these resolutions. I say that it is most remarkable that, with the exception of the remarks of the gentleman to whom I have referred, we have . not been favoured with any statement from members of the Government who are on the inside and who should know something about this matter. I do think that we are entitled to more information along these lines than we have received up to the present time.
I feel that it is unnecessary that I should say anything uncomplimentary about Mackenzie and MJann or about any other person in discussing these resolutions; nor do I (think it is necessary that members of the Government should spend so much time in eulogizing these two wizards of finance, as they are called; these two empire builders; these two men who have devoted their lives to making Canada the great

and prosperous country that it is to-day. This is purely a financial transaction; it is purely a question of whether, in the first place, we should give aid to the Canadian Northern system, and whether, in the second place, the Government are proposing to give this aid in .a manner which will be in the (best interests of the people of the country as a whole. Therefore, as I have said, I am here neither to praise nor to condemn Mackenzie and Mann; I am here to discuss, very briefly indeed, the financial position in which I find this company placed to-day, and in which I find the Government placed by reason of their yielding to the solicitations of these two railway magnates. I know that we cannot find in Canada another instance of where two men have accomplished such wonders in the financial world as have Mackenzie and Mann in connection with the Canadian Northern railway system; in fact, I doubt very much whether the case has a parallel on the American continent. Just think of what they have accomplished. Without putting in one 4 p.m. dollar of private funds; without [DOT] becoming responsible for the payment of one dollar; without doing anything but beg from everybody whom they met, these two gentlemen have succeeded in getting from the people of Canada, from the Dominion and from the provinces, over $200,000,000 either of money or of money's worth. I say that this is something unique in the history of Canada, and, I believe, in the history of the American continent: over $200,000,000 in hard cash begged from the people of Canada, who were cajoled, and, in some cases, I am afraid, almost threatened into giving this money in order to enrich these gentlemen and make them a pair of millionaires. When hon. gentlemen opposite talk about Mackenzie and Mann being patriots, I am almost compelled to say something unpleasant. My hon. friend the Solicitor General smiles; it is no wonder, because I am afraid that the intercourse which my hon. friend hag* had with these gentlemen and their solicitor during the last two months has given him an insight into the real condition of affairs which makes him smile in his sleep when Mackenzie and Mann appear to him in his dreams. When attorneys and counsel come into court with a case they take it as it is presented to them and make the best they can of it, and I think that my hon. friend the Solicitor General, who always makes the 
best of a bad case, bias done the beat he could in this case. iBut my hon. friend knows that so much of this story has not been told that he cannot help smiling when the names of Mackenzie and Mann are mentioned to him.
These men have been referred to as patriots: these men who have almost buccaneered $200,000,000 out of the people of Canada. I went over the matter very hurriedly a few moments ago and, according to the figures which the Government have given us, we find that Mackenzie and Mann have obtained, in the first place, over $25,000,000 in cash and, in the second place, lands in the Northwest which they admit are worth $30,000,000. Further, they have obtained the guarantee of bonds and securities by the Dominion Government to the extent of $58,000,000 and by the provincial Governments to the extent of $76,000,000. This makes a total of $180,000,000 in round figures. In addition to that, they have lands in the provinces of Quebec, Ontario and Nova Scotia, roads which have been built and purchased by them-but all of which have been (built practically by public money-all over the eastern portion of Canada and, to some extent, in the province of Manitoba; roads built in the province of Quebec and in the province of Nova Scotia. Adding the sum total of the value of these properties you find that at least $220,000,000 or $225,000,000 of actual money or moneys worth has been given to these two gentlemen for the purpose of building this railway system. They conceived, perhaps, one of the boldest schemes which was ever thought of in America. Two men, who at the time had, I imagine, very few dollars of private funds, but who did not put in a dollar, no matter what they may have had, conceived the idea of building a great transcontinental railway. We are told that we should consider them as patriots because they 'had imagination sufficient to induce them to go into this great scheme. I do not suppose that there is a member in this House who has not had sufficient imagination during his lifetime to induce him to go into some financial scheme or other. Some of them, I presume, have turned out satisfactorily; many of them have turned out unsatisfactorily. I know that I have gone into financial schemes during my lifetime; many of them, I am sorry to say, turned out unsatisfactorily, but probably the schemes that other members and I myself have entered into are just as important so far as our communities are concerned as is

the Mackenzie and Mann scheme so far as Canada is concerned. But when our schemes go wrong, do we go to our municipal authorities, to our city and town councils or to our provincial Governments and say: We conceived the idea of establishing a great institution of some' kind, but the thing 'has gone wrong; we are up against the wall. It is true that we have spent not a dollar of our own money; it is true that we 'have spent all the money that we have been able to borrow; it is true that we have spent all the money which the people have given us, that we cannot borrow more and that nobody will give us any more money. We cannot go on with this work; therefore it is up to you to finance it for us. Would our people call us patriots, call us magnates, if we did this, or would they call us idiots? I have been all through the mill ; I have had financial transactions that have gone bad but I did not find any government or corporation or municipality coming to my aid and putting up thousands of dollars for me. They say:	If you are fool enough
to undertake a thing that you cannot carry through, put up your own money, put up your own securities; if you cannot pay your way, go to the wall, and let somebody else take it up. That is what you find in the ordinary affairs of life, that is what probably one-half the members of this House have found in ordinary business experience. The hon. member for Lambton says that these gentlemen are patriots and are absolutely bankrupt. The words he used were:	They have gone to the extent
of their credit, then he says there is no other source to which they can go for money except the Dominion Government; and because these men are bankrupt, and because there is no other source to which they can go, and because they come here and ask us to grant them an enormous sum of money, it is our duty to grant it. This is the logic, and I think the hon. member for Lambton pretty nearly stated the logic of all the members on the Government side of this House who have supported this measure up to the present time. Perhaps you might say that it would be only fair that I should state what my own views are on this matter, and for fear that ony one should claim that I am not frank in discussing it, I wish to admit that this matter has assumed such gigantic proportions that I do not see how the Government of Canada can do otherwise than do something in order to prevent the
enterprise going entirely to smash, because that would be a very serious matter for Canada. But when I say that, I am not agreeing in any manner whatever to the scheme proposed by the Government in order to work out a solution to this very unfortunate condition of affairs.
I now want to discuss very briefly the scheme proposed by the Government. A large number of documents have been laid upon the table of the House. Some of these have been printed in a blue-book and some have not. I do not think that I have spent more real time in trying to understand any subject that has come before the House since I have been in Parliament than I have spent on this Canadian Northern scheme; and I am compelled to admit, although it may not be very much of a compliment to my ability, that I have rarely attempted to speak upon a matter about which I could so little understand many things connected with it. If there is any more light to be thrown upon these things, it is the duty of the Government to give us more explicit explanation than we have received. In so far as I have .been able to go, and I have read over every word in the blue book and every document laid upon the table of the House, I find that there are present liabilities upon this road amounting to about $42,540,000, not for the purpose of building the road, not to extend the road, not to complete the system, but to pay their debts and put them in a position where it will be safe to run engines and cars over the road. That is the position as I find it, if I am right in my figures. I have made up these figures largely from sessional paper N'o. 269 I, a portion of Which has been printed and a portion not. It is easy to say, produce your proof. There will be a demand for additional branch lines-a perfectly proper demand, which must be complied: with-, which will cost the Dominion Government millions of dollars. Would it not be better to take the railroad over now than to allow these men to manipulate this $100,000,000 of funds for three or four years longer, and then come back and say: We cannot carry it on any longer, we must have further aid or you must take it over. What happens when we do take it over? If there was one portion of the address of my hon. friend from Calgary which impressed me more than anything else, it was that in which he described the foreclosure of this mortgage. I thought that my hon. friend got down to the existing facts and to real human nature a little closer than in any other portion of his great speech. As the hon. member for Montreal, St. Antoine (Mr. Ames), stated: It is true these men have been pretty bold actors; it is true these men have had very grave charges laid against them; it is true these men have

been tried by the Government and have been found wanting, but we are going to give them one more chance, and, if they default again, down comes the axe and off go their heads. 'Balk about toying to foreclose this mortgage; you would see a lobby around here such as had never been heard of in Canada before. There would not be a contractor, a [business man, a politician, anybody in Canada who had ever done business with these people but would be brought here in order to appeal to hon. gentlemen opposite to prevent this taking place. In the end, if it did take place, instead of foreclosing on $60,000,000 worth of stock we would be more likely to have to pay them $15,000,000 or $25,000,000 to get rid of them. That is the true inwardness of giving them this $60,000,000 of stock. It gives them absolute control of this money; it gives them the right to manage the business; it gives them the right to keep rates up against the western producer, and, more than that, if we want to attempt to foreclose this mortgage, it will give them the right to come here and demand from $15,000,000 to $25,000,000 in payment for their equity.
Would my hon. friend prefer the ordinary methods of foreclosing mortgages as embodied in the agreement of 1911?
I prefer the kind of agreement that the Government entered into with the Canadian Pacific railway thirty years ago.

I am asking my hon. friend if he would prefer the ordinary methods of 1911?
Mr. OARVlELL: My hon. friend must remember that in 1911, when we guaranteed the bonds, we had a mortgage upon this road. We had a security that there was something in; we had something which noibody could allow to be foreclosed. But here my hon. friend has as security merely a bankrupt concern. My hon. friend is putting up $45,000,000 when he knows that there is not more than 75 or 50 per cent of actual value behind it. There is as much difference between the North Pole and the South Pole as between the deal in 1911 and that in 1914. If my hon. friend wants a parallel, let him go back to the agreement with the Canadian Pacific railway in 1884. When the Canadian Pacific railway came here and said: We are up against the wall; we cannot

sell our bonds and we cannot get any more money, Sir John Macdonald did not say: We-will foreclose this mortgage if you come back to Parliament again, hut Sir John Macdonald and the Conservative party of that day provided that automatically all their rights, all their equity of redemption, -were gone if they defaulted upon the bonds.
After a year.

Yes, after a year. My hon. friend provides that there cannot be any default for three years. They can go on and ask the Dominion of Canada to pay the interest for three years, and they will ask us to pay every cent of it. We do not give them only $45,000,000, but we are compelled to pay the interest on that amount for three years, and all they have to do is to pay the interest upon the rest of the securities. After three years, if the interest is not paid upon these or any other securities, we cannot forclose them; we cannot cut their heads off, but they will simply come back to Parliament, and we are going to go through all this lobby again that many of us here have been watching for the last three months. We shall again have the lobby at work, but to a much greater degree than we have had it before, and, instead of foreclosing their equity, we will be compelled to pay them an enormous amount of money to get rid of them I have taken longer than I had intended, but this subject is so fascinating that one is apt to be carried away by it. When you see the blunders made by hon. gentlemen opposite, when you see how Mr. Z. A. Lash has taken these hon. gentlemen into camp and disposed of the whole of them, when you see the great benefits that he will get out of it as contrasted with what we get out of it, if you have any interest in this country you must find it a fascinating subject. I have tried to point out that we are not giving Mackenzie and Mann enough money to finish this road. We are only giving them money enough to pay their debts, and, worse than that, we are allowing them to handle this money and to pay these debts themselves. We are giving them the right to pay construction accounts about which we know nothing. We are giving them the right to use this money for betterments about which we know nothing. W7e are giving them the right to the use of this money and to the use of it at once, and yet the road will be left in the same position as it is. I do not know where

they are going to get money, but if they can get the money, we are giving them the right to go on and finish the road which will take from $25,000,000 to $40,000,000 more. We are giving them the right to take $35,000,000 more out of the people and they own the road, or they own 60 per cent of it while we own 40 per cent. We are giving them the right to control freight rates and to keep them at any point they have a mind to. We are assuming (the responsibility not only of paying $400,000,000 of a mortgage, but of paying the interest and of the foreclosure of these securities as they mature.
I say that we ought to have some light on this subject. We ought to "have an investigation. We ought to know where the money has gone and to whom it has gone,
[DOT] how much has gone into the railway and how much into somebody's pocket. We want to know how much these two gentlemen have got out of it. We are giving them $60,000,000 of stock and up to the present time not one dollar of their own has gone into it. We ought to have an investigation into that. We ought to know what the road has cost. We ought to know what it is going to cost to complete the system, what it is going to cost to build new branch lines and where this money is going. Then, Sir, I am satisfied that the condition of affairs will not only be shown to be bad, but that it will be shown to be so bad that this company will be compelled to come back to this Parliament in two years from now and ask for further advances. My hon. friends opposite ought to give us some light upon these matters, they ought to have an investigation and find out the true condition of affairs and, if they are as we suspect they are, they ought to eliminate these two men. I am not finding fault with Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann; they are big actors, they are men who have played the game and lost. They gambled in the biggest way that men ever did in the Dominion of Canada. They gambled and lost, and now my hon. friends come to the rescue and say: Let them go on and gamble and win. If my hon. friends opposite are putting up. the money to help them to gamble, we should have the equity and not they, and that would mean that the people of Canada would get it.
While I have never been very much enamoured of government ownership, and while I would not look forward to the adoption of that principle with any great degree of comfort, still I would rather see this
handed over to a commission to be operated by this Government than that it should be handed over to these two gentlemen. It is better for us, it is better for the people, ft is better for the farmers in the western country to reduce the freight rates on the system, because it will not have earned sufficient money to pay dividends. You give Mackenzie and Mann this $60,000,000 of stock and you are compelled to keep the rates where they can earn dividends. If you take over the road, and if you put it in the hands of a commission, you can run it as you are running the Intercolonial railway-at cost. You do not have to earn dividends, you only have to charge sufficient rates to pay the fixed charges, and while you are bringing down the rates on the Canadian Northern railway you are at the same time bringing down the rates on the Canadian Pacific railway and Grand Trunk Pacific. You give the people transportation at the cheapest possible cost under existing circumstances. For these reasons, and considering the -very great paucity of information we possess, the terrible responsibilities we assume, and the condition of affairs which is likely to ensue, I shall have great pleasure in voting for the amendment of my hon. friend from Pictou,

speakeroldname: Hon. W. T. WHITE (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must crave the indulgence of the House; a bronchial cold has almost robbed me of my voice and what I have to say must necessarily be said briefly. My hon. friend (Mr. Carvell) has commented upon the fact that hitherto no minister other than the Prime Minister has spoken on this question, but that only goes to show how unreasonable my hon. friend can be at times. It shows his lack of appreciation of a very delicate compliment on our part, because we desired to have the benefit of the lucubrations of the hon. gentleman from Oarleton on this question. We knew he would illumine it. It is not my intention to follow him in his excursion into the realm of figures. My hon. friend is always interesting as a dialectician, but as a mathematician he is a hopeless failure. His literary training I think was reasonably good, but he has grave cause for dissatisfaction with the teacher of his youth who instructed him in arithmetic. I have no doubt the Solicitor General will straighten out all the tangles which befog his brain when we get into Committee on the Resolution.
The issue before the House is simple: shall the Government afford aid to the

Canadian Northern system? Is this the time to afford it, and if so have we adopted the best method of affording it, and has the public interest been sufficiently safeguarded by the proposals of the Government? These are in general terms the questions which are involved in the consideration of the resolutions now before the House.
It is customary in dealing with financial legislation affecting railways to dilate upon the importance to the people of Canada of the transportation problem. That problem is of vital and paramount importance; it is common ground to both political parties, and there is no necessity to touch upon it now.
There is another question which has been much controverted;-has our railway policy in Canada been mistaken; have we aimed too high; have we sought to accomplish too much; have we, as has been said by some, one transcontinental railway too many in Canada? Are there too many lines traversing the north shore of lake Superior?
Much can be said for this view, but the time has gene by for debating the question. We have three transcontinental railway systems, one the greatest in the world; the other two nearing completion. The past is irrevocable. The book is closed, no matter whether its pages may have been writ well or writ ill. The die has been cast, and we have to deal with the situation as we find it. Whether mistakes have been made or have not been made, it is idle now to discuss. It is, in my judgment, the wisest policy to make the best of things, to accept what is inevitable, and above all to strongly believe that with courage and with hope and with resolution affairs can be made to work out satisfactorily. I firmly believe that the railway situation of Canada will work out. This country has resources illimitable; wealth beyond the dreams of avarice for those who will succeed in it. The various geographical sections of Canada are empires in extent, and variety of natural production capable of sustaining a population many times as numerous as that we have inhabiting our Dominion to-day. Is the population of Canada to remain fixed, crystallized, and stereotyped, and is the transportation policy of Canada to have regard to the present only? Is imagination to play no part in our policy? Must the railway follow the plough rather than the plough the railway? Would the Canadian Pacific railway ever have been constructed had the vision of its builders seen only the

population of the eighties? Would the Northwest be the Northwest of to-day, or the boundless and barren prairie of years ago, had it not been for the vision of statesmen and of railway builders who, with enterprise unparalleled, have carried their lines of railway to its uttermost parts, bringing colonization and civilization in their train? Situated as we are geographically, what has the opening of the West meant to the Bast? I say, Sir, that it has meant advantage incalculable. We have manifold return for the money spent in railway development, even though millions may have been needlessly and mistakenly expended. We are only on the threshold of our great adventure in the extension of civilization to the vast plains of the Canadian West.
Shall we stop now? Shall we lose courage upon the very verge of success? Shall we lose sight of the millions of population still to come? As for me, I have an abiding faith in the destiny of this country. No other creed can permanently be in keeping with the spirit, the determination, and the aspirations of the Canadian people. Parliament, I am sure, will never be wanting in imagination in dealing with the larger problems of this great Dominion.
Now, Mr. Speaker, what is the existing railway situation in Canada? What is the situation with which this Government has found itself confronted? We have had to finish the eastern section of the National Transcontinental railway; the money has been found and will be found as required. The road is almost completed. The year before we came into power the late Government had taken a step which determined that the Canadian Northern railway should be a transcontinental system, by guaranteeing securities to the extent of $35,000,000 upon the line of the Canadian Northern Ontario Railway, from Montreal	to Port	Arthur.Construction upon this and other lines of the Canadian Northern Ontario was well advanced. There was then the action of the Government of British Columbia in guaranteeing securities upon the line of the	Canadian	NorthernPacific, which	was then	under
way through the Rocky mountains from the Yellowhead Pass to New Westminster, a most expensive line, costing in some places $100,000 per mile. During our first year in office we granted a subsidy at the rate of $12,000 per mile to this line, and I say that if under any circumstances

whatever railway subsidies are justifiable, the subsidy of $12,000 per mile which we granted to the Canadian Northern Pacific in respect to its lines through the Rocky mountains, was abundantly justified. This brings me to the year 1913, a year of stress, a year of strain, a period of financial stringency the most severe-
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend may laugh. I do not know whether he understands the severity of the financial stringency, the most severe, the most widespread, that has been experienced I believe during the lifetime of any member of this House. That stringency was due to world-wide causes which stopped the supply of capital at its source, the great international money centres, causing retrenchment and embarrassment to enterprises in all parts of the world. It was in this posture, in this extremity of affairs that the Canadian Northern Railway Company last year made application for aid by way of subsidy and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company for aid made application by way of loan. The subsidy in the one case amounted to thirteen or fourteen million dollars and the loan amounted to fifteen million dollars. The subsidies were given by this Government and the loan was made. Had the Government not taken the action it did, railway construction must have ceased in Canada upon the two lines in question. What the result would have been to Canadian securities in London and, by consequence, upon Canadian credit and prosperity, I leave to the imagination of this House. There is no need to apologize, and I do not apologize for the action of the Government last year. I say that it was strong, courageous, timely, necessary action. Had it not been taken, those of the public who have criticised us for taking it would have to-day execrated us for not having taken it. In connection with these subsidies, we obtained stock in the Canadian Northern Railway Company to the extent of $7,000,000, par value. My hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald), for whom I always cherish, as he knows, a high, regard, the other evening indulged in some caustic witticism at my expense with reference to the issue of the stock certificate covering these 70,000 shares. That is what the hon. member from Calgary (Mr. Bennett) said. I just adopted his statement.

No.

My hon. friend says that they turned on the printing press in order to print a stock certificate. There was absolutely no deception of this House on the part of either the Canadian Northern Railway Company or Mackenzie, Mann and Company. The Subsidy Bill showed as clearly as words could show the intention of the Government, the intention of Parliament, in the legislation relating to the issue of the 70,000 shares of the Canadian Northern Railway Company stock, that it was in part consideration of the subsidy which the Government was granting to the system. I am going to put on ' Hansard,' because this matter has been discussed very widely, and because some most unjust statements have been made respecting the Canadian Northern Railway Company with regard to the issue of this certificate, sections 8 and 9 of the Subsidy Act of last session, which is a* follows:
8.	No subsidy shall be granted under this Act unless and until there shall have been issued and transferred upon the books of the Canadian Northern Railway Company to the Minister of Finance and Receiver General of Canada, in trust for His Majesty, shares in the common stock of the Canadian Northern Railway Company of the par value of $7,000,000, which said stock and all rights appurtenant thereto shall be held for the benefit of His Majesty absolutely, and shall be deemed to be fully paid up, non-assessable and not subject to calls; provided that the said stock or any part thereof may be disposed of under the authority ot Parliament upon such terms and conditions as it may determine and the proceeds of the sale thereof paid into the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada.

What was the position? The Government of Canada gave $15,000,000 by way of subsidy to the Canadian Northern Railway system, and the Canadian Northern in part consideration issued $7,000,000 par value of fully paid shares of its stock. If any stock in the world was fully paid, that was, because it was paid in full in part consideration of the subsidy granted by Parliament to the Canadian Northern system. I wish to clear up that point, because a great deal too much has been made of it.

Will my hon. friend go on record as telling the House and the country last year that the stock he was getting, apart from the technical interpretation of the Act, was entirely new stock that was to be issued, or that it was to be part of the stock already in existence?

speechtext: I certainly didi not tell the House or the country that it was part of the stock already existing.
You did not tell the House that it was not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The legislation was before the House. It was open to my hon. friends. Every section in the Act, including the two sections I have read, were discussed in committee. When the
House rose at six o'clock, I was dealing with the railway situation with which we were confronted, I said that we had to deal with a condition and not a hypothesis. The Canadian Northern Railway system requires $100,000,000 to complete it3 enterprise. It is prepared to provide $58,000,000 and it has asked the Government of Canada to provide the additional $42,000,000 by guarantee of an issue of 4 per cent bonds of the par value of $45,000,000, which may be expected to realize in the neighbourhood of the required $42,000,000. The question, therefore, before the House is whether we shall grant the aid which is sought by the Canadian Northern Railway system or allow it to go into default. Let us consider (for a moment the railway system in question. It has main lines extending from Quebec to Vancouver. It has feeders in almost every province. It has the constituent and subsidiary companies specified in the schedules to the resolutions, exceeding, I think, thirty in all, a system of railway, express, transfer, telegraph, steamship, land and tunnel and terminal companies. It represents at present 7,000 miles of railroad and when it is completed it will represent 10,000 miles. Upon this system some $300,000,000 of securities have been issued and it is to-day confronted, as I have said, with the necessity of obtaining further aid from the Government of Canada or a receivership. A system so vast and complicated as the Canadian Northern Railway system has necessarily involved itself with the vita] interests of the country and we find iron and steel companies, rolling stock companies, supply companies, great mercantile and manufacturing establishments, all dependent in some measure, and some in large measure, upon the continuance of the immense activities of this system. The Canadian Northern Railway system has received sums exceeding $20,000,000 in subsidies, has received in guarantees some $130,000,000 from the federal and provincial governments, and has raised in the neighbourhood of $170,000,000 on its own securities. Almost every province in Canada has pledged its credit in connection with the securities of this road and therefore we have the situation that, by reason of the interest which 248
they have in this system, the Dominion and provincial governments and the industrial and other establishments I have mentioned, are all vitally interested in this company and its system being maintained as a going concern. Of its securities there are hundreds of millions upon the London and European markets. It has done much to develop the West, and the West to-day is calling for more rolling stock, for better service and for extension of the Canadian Northern railway to the unsettled districts. The question, therefore, which we have to determine, and which the Government has determined, is whether this system, which is on the very verge of completion, shall be allowed to default on its securities and go into the hands of a receiver. I say that no thinking man in Canada can answer that question in the affirmative. I say it is unthinkable that the Canadian Northern railway, with these thirty subsidiary companies, railway, express, telegraph, steamship line and terminal companies, shall be allowed to go into the hands of a receiver, having regard to the interest that I have described of the Dominion and of the provincial governments in the road, and to the importance of the continuance of the activities of this system to all the manufacturing and business interests in Canada. Can the matter be allowed to stand for six months? I say the answer to that is supplied by the financial statement which has been laid upon the table. I say that prompt and immediate action by the Government and by Parliament is required in this matter. It is true that this road has been generously helped by the Dominion and other governments in Canada, in other words by the public, in the past. My hon. friend from Carleton (Mr. Carvell) this afternoon said that they had 'buccaneered ' $200,000,000 out	of the people of Canada.
Well, they have not buccaneered any such sum out of the people of Canada since this Government has been in power. I would like to point out to my hon. friend that the late Government gave guarantees to the Canadian Northern railway to about $58,000,000. One of the last acts of the late Government was to give a guarantee of $35,000,000 upon the securities of the Canadian Northern Ontario line from Montreal to. Port Arthur. That sum is only $10,000,000 less than the guarantee that we are giving to-day, so that if the promoters of this road have buccaneered the people of Canada out of $200,000,000, my hon. friend must assume responsibility

for his share of complicity in respect to the guarantees so given.
There has been a great deal of confusion of thought in this matter. Attention has been fixed upon Mackenzie and Mann. I desire to say that Mackenzie and Mann as individuals are of absolutely no interest or concern to this Government. ,If the question at issue related only to the advantage or disadvantage of Mackenzie and Mann the Government would not waste a moment upon it. The only basis of the action of the Government is the interests of the people of Canada, and I say that it is in the interests of the people of Canada that this system-the Canadian Northern with all its subsidiary and constituent companies, 7,000 miles of completed line, and, later on, 10,000 miles-should receive the aid which it seeks in order that the road may be completed. The personal vicissitudes of Mackenzie and Mann, enterprising railway builders as they have been, are of no interest to us; if no public interest were at stake there would be no basis for action on the part of the Government. I repeat that the foundation of the action of the Government in this matter is the public interest. It is in the interests of the people of Canada that this vast system should be completed, linked up, and made productive.
There is another consideration. Shall we allow the general credit of Canada to he impaired in the London market by default on the part of this railway company, and shall the provinces he1 called upon for their guarantees? That is a question of interest to every member of this House. I have heard men speak lightly of putting a system like this into a receivership. Considering the many classes of securities which have been issued by this company, ranking as they do in their several orders, I put forward the assertion that in the event of a receivership for this system it would be years before the road was on its feet again. Does any member of tnis House seriously say that a receivership of this complicated body of corporate enterprises could he carried out without enormous legal and other costs, and without a most injurious influence upon the business of this country as a whole, because you find this company's lines in every province, and I have explained that this Government and the provincial governments, and all the manufacturing and mercantile establishments of Canada, are interested in the continuance of the

activities of this system. I sometimes think we do not realize how vastly complicated a system the Canadian Northern railway is. I say, therefore, that if any other solution can be found a receivership should be unthinkable, and I am glad that my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) and other gentlemen opposite agree with	me	in	that. I say,	andthey	say,	that	the road must	goon	to	completion in	the interestsof the people of Canada. In the case of a single corporation where no question would arise as to constituent or subsidiary companies a receivership would be serious, but it	would be	infinitely more seriouswhere	you	have	not one company	buttwenty or thirty to be dealt with under the slow process of a receivership. Only one thing could happen:	The dispersal or disintegration of the whole system. Even with the Government as a receiver, as one hon. gentleman has suggested, damage beyond repair would be done to the credit of the company.
The Government has given the question prolonged and painstaking attention and consideration. I venture to say that no question that has ever come before a government of Canada has received more profound and more serious consideration than this application of the Canadian Northern Railway Company for aid. Upon a review of the whole situation, of all the considerations involved, we have come to the conclusion that I believe every thinking man has come to who has had the facts before him that it is the clear duty of the Dominion of Canada to come to the assistance of the Canadian Northern Railway Company. We were not without precedents for such action. As I have said, in 1911, the Government under the leadership of the right hon. leader of the Opposition gave the Canadian Northern railway a guarantee to the extent of $35,000,000 upon its line from Montreal to Port Arthur, and when they did that they cast the die that determined the Canadian Northern railway as one of the transcontinental systems of Canada. My hon. friend from Garleton talks about ' buccaneering ' the country by getting these guarantees. Did he protest in 1911 against that $35,000,000 guarantee? Where, where was Roderick then? He may have been in the House, but he did not act like Roderick;. So far as I can make out, he said very little.

We have, therefore, taken a charge upon the stocks; we have taken a charge upon the undertaking of the Canadian Northern proper. Further than that, this money is to be used for the purpose of completing several constituent undertakings, and the further provision is made that to the extent that this money is used for the construction and betterment and improvement of these constituent railways, a charge shall be taken back upon their physical assets, upon their corporate undertakings, to the trustee as part of the mortgage premises which we shall have as security for this $45,000,000 guarantee. In addition to that, we have insisted that the Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, shall pledge as part of the mortgage premises $10,000,000 of stock of the town site companies connected with the Canadian Northern Railway system.
The hon. member for Welland (Mr. German)-I am sorry that he is not here tonight, because he has a strong, vigorous, masculine understanding-spoke about taking a mortgage upon an insolvent concern, and I think the hon. member for Carleton also said something along that line. I would like to cite an illustration-and the hon. member for Carleton will appreciate the point as quickly as anybody will-

drawn from a situation that is close to the hon. member for Welland. Let us assume that the development of power by a great power company at Niagara Falls is to cost $10,000,000 before it is completed and becomes profitable or fruitful. Let us say that, by reason of some financial or other conditions, after expending $5,000,000 they find themselves unable to pay their contractors and to raise additional money, and have to seek assistance from bankers. If they do not obtain that assistance, what is their position? The enterprise is confronted with a receivership. But would anybody call that an insolvent concern? Would it not rather be said that if they could obtain the additional $5,000,000, the enterprise, would be able to pay the interest upon the cost of installation and possibly produce dividends upon stock? The cases are not quite analogous, but I would point out to my hon. friend that one reason and one justification for our action so far as security is concerned is this: that if by the joining up of these isolated or detached links of the Canadian Northern Railway system the Canadian Northern gets a transcontinental line with all its feeders in full operation, what at present looks like a losing venture may and probably will be turned into profitable enterprise. It is commonplace to remark that if you have a railway system consisting of isolated units scattered throughout a country as large as Europe, it is not to be supposed that you are going to get the earning power before these units are joined up; you do not get the earning power until they are all linked up and in this case it is to link up and to complete these undertakings that this aid is required. They cannot become fully productive: they cannot pay their fixed charges; they cannot yield any profit to capital invested in them; they cannot serve the people of Canada until they are all joined together and until the system is in operation as a transcontinental road, serving the people of Canada to the best of its capacity both as to through and local traffic.

I am dealing with the disposition of the proceeds of these guaranteed securities, and I say to the hon. member for Carleton that if he looks at the measure introduced by the hon. member for South Renfrew, then Minister of Railways, in 1911, he will find the words almost identical:
The forms and terms of the new trust deed, and the times and manner of the issue of the guaranteed securities, and the dispositions of the moneys to be raised thereon by sale, pledge or otherwise, and the forms and manner of guarantee or guarantees shall be such as the Governor in Council approves, and such terms, provisions and conditions as the Governor in Council may consider expedient or necessary shall be included In the new trust deed.
What does that mean? It means that these moneys will be paid out for the purpose for which they have been provided according to the terms of this resolution, that they will be paid out according to the provisions of a trust mortgage which will ensure control of their destination in the hands of the Government. We pay out money from month to month under the Canadian Northern Ontario Railway mortgage which was given to the Government in respect of the $35,000 a mile guarantee on that line of which I am speaking. How is it done? All possible safeguards are thrown around it. I have taken great pains to inquire from the Railway Department how the inspection is made on the strength of which the certificates are given upon which the Finance Department acts

in paying out these moneys in connection with the issue of $35,000,000 upon the Canadian Northern Ontario Railway line. The proceeds went into a bank, and have been checked out in the last two years. There are several millions lying to the credit of the account to-day which will become available in due course for the completion of the line in respect of which the guaranteed securities were issued. The inspecting engineer of the railway with the chief engineer goes carefully into the question of the cost of construction of the line. He sees the profile, he knows the quantities, he makes his calculation, he estimates that the line will cost so many million dollars, let us say $45,000,000, between Montreal and Port Arthur. The guarantee is at the rate of $35,000 a mile. Let us say that yields $31,000 a mile, because it is a three and one-half per cent security. Now, when $2,000,000 worth of work has been done on the construction of that line from Montreal to Port Arthur, the inspecting engineer certifies, after making his inspection, to the chief engineer. The chief engineer, after giving the matter his attention, reports to the Minister of Railways that $2,000,000 of work has been done upon that line; that the total cost of the line will be, let us assume, $45,000 per mile; that the proceeds of the guaranteed securities is only $31,000 a mile, and that therefore the road is entitled to have paid out of the proceeds standing to the credit of the Minister of Finance and Receiver General, thirty-one forty-fifths of $2,000,000. I ask if there could be any greater safeguard thrown by Parliament around a situation of that kind, that is if you can rely upon your officials? You have your inspecting engineer taking out his quantities, making his calculations, and saying that the road will cost so much, whether built by Mackenzie and Mann or by anybody else. You have, in addition to that, the chief engineer revising his work, and reporting to the minister and, finally, there is paid out only the proportion that the amount realized of that $35,000 of securities per mile bears to the actual cost, the $45,000 per mile which has been assumed to be the cost arrived at by the engineer. Therefore, so far as the destination of this money is concerned, hon. gentlemen opposite did not worry in 1911, and here are provisions identical with those of the statute of 1911, under which these moneys will be paid out. The same officials are going to make the inspections and reports.
