Then I ask: Will the hon. member for Edmonton, or any other hon. member in this House, stand up and affirm this transaction in every other respect, but say: Give back the $40,000,000 of stock to Mackenzie and Mann? I do not believe there is a man who will stand up and

say: I affirm the transaction in every other respect; give back the stock; give your guarantees but by no means take this fully-paid common stock; we agree you should give the guarantee but thrust back upon Mackenzie and Mann the thirty-three million dollars of common stock. I tell you, you will make two hearts beat as one if you could induce the Government to do that; there will be two glad men in Canada if the thirty-three million dollars are thrust back upon them by a reluctant and unwilling government, and these two men are Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann. But neither my hon. friend nor any other man dare stand up and tell the people of Canada that he affirms this transaction in regard to the guarantees and at the same time that he will not have placed in the Dominion treasury the forty million dollars of common stock.
The railway legislation of this country in the past has been fatuous in the extreme. I admire the enterprise of the Canadian Pacific railway. One of the most marvellous transactions in the history of the world was the carrying out of the Canadian Pacific railway in the eighties, linking up the East and West, rounding up Confederation and making it possible. These men had courage. But supposing the Government of that time, in consideration of what had been done for the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, had said: we will take forty million or fifty million dollars of stock in the Canadian Pacific railway, what would the result be to-day. Suppose the Grand Trunk Pacific should turn out to be the great success my right hon. friend prophesied for it when he brought down his legislation; suppose it come up to the vision of his imagination which he has told us of on more than one occasion, and suppose the right hon. gentleman when he brought in the legislation had said he would take for the Dominion treasury twenty-five million dollars of the stock of the Grand Trunk Pacific, would there be any wrong in his doing that? I think not. Let me say to my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) that notwithstanding what he says about the undesirability of the Government of Canada becoming a partner with a railway company, the Government of Canada in a sense has become a partner with the Grand Trunk Pacific, and on a much more logical basis than the holding of common stock, because if he will turn to the National Transcontinental Railway agreement ne will find that the Government of Canada appoints a direc-

tor on the Grand Trunk Pacific. Am I right?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
And yet my hon. friend
now holds up both hands in holy horror and says: do not be a partner with shareholders in these railway enterprises, but at the same time he defends the action of the Government of which he was a member in nominating a director of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. Surely we have reduced the argument about partnership to an absolute absurdity.
I say that the people of this country would never hear of the Government giving back this stock. If this enterprise succeeds that stock will become valuable; if this enterprise does not succeed notwithstanding the aid we are affording it, then of course we have incurred the risk and will have to take over the system. And if we did not take the common stock and it succeeded, the beneficiaries of our action which will enable the Canadian Northern to complete its enterprise, would not be the people of Canada-our action would result only in the aggrandizement of Mackenzie and Mann, the holders of $100,000,000 of common stock, $40,000,000 of which the Government is taking and leaving them $60,000,000. As I said, if our credit saves the road, then Mackenzie and Mann should not be the beneficiaries alone, but the people of Canada should share in whatever benefit will come to the stockholders in this great enterprise.
My hon. friend (Mr. Carvell) was greatly concerned about the freight rates and he said: it follows as the night the day that if you take this forty million dollars of fully paid stock of the Canadian Northern you are going to prevent the freight rates from being reduced. Remember, he is dealing with two situations: one in which we do not take the stock and the other in which we do take it. If we do not take it Mackenzie and Mann will have $100,000,000-
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: How much will they have?
I would give them about $10,000,000 of stock in that agreement.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I did not think my hon.
friend would be so generous as to give them $10,000,000 stock, but he was more generous to the Grand Trunk when he allowed them to get $25,000,000 in consideration of their guarantee. I am afraid my hon. friend
(Mr. Carvell) is not consistent. His argument this afternoon went along the line: if you do take this stock then you are in a much worse position than if you do not; if you have the $40,000,000 of stock the people of Canada will be in a much worse position as to freight rates than if the Government did not take the stock. But if that were the only thing in the world that stood in the reduction of freight rates, I could understand some big Prime Minister o\ Canada saying: if our $40,000,000 of stock stands in the way of a reduction in freight rates then we can do several things with it: we can, for example, surrender it for cancellation if we want to. So that my hon. friend need not worry about the Government going to impose burdens on the people of Canada by holding $40,000,000 of Canadian Northern fully-paid up stock. And if that contingency does not arise which he dreads, then the Government of Canada will hold	this	$40,000,000	of fullypaid	up	stock in the	Canadian
Northern, and they will be able to take whatever benefits may come from that ownership. Then the hon. gentleman asks: What would happen if Mackenzie and Mann should come back? Well, there are the resolutions, and hon. gentlemen can interpret them just as well as we can. I know what power we have under these resolutions in case of default, in case of receivership, in case of the road being unable to carry on its enterprise. It means that the Government of Canada could at once enter possession of the whole line, to be disposed of as Parliament may direct at its next session. I say that this is the most progressive legislation that has ever been introduced into this Parliament affecting the giving of any guarantees or aid to any railway company.
Now, Mr. Speaker, when I started out I said I had been suffering from a severe bronchial cold, which has almost deprived me of the power of speech; but my hon. friend from Carleton (Mr. Carvell) seems to have stimulated me to super-exertion, and I have spoken at much greater length than I had originally intended. It only shows the resources of the human voice when it is properly exercised and in a good cause, as this is. I remember that the late Sir John Macdonald once expressively said that a parliamentary speech should be animated conversation. In the remarks which I have addressed to the House this afternoon I have been grave and gay by turns.
I desire now, at the end, to be serious

because this is one of the most important questions that has ever been before the Government or the Parliament of Canada. We realized that when it was first presented for our consideration, and, speaking for myself, and speaking for the Prime Minister, because I know the earnest, painstaking, and sleepless consideration he has given to this matter, I say that no question which has ever come up in Canadian politics has been given more full, more sincere, or more conscientious consideration than these resolutions which are now before this House. We have not had to deal with an hypothesis, we have had to deal with an actual condition. It is easy to criticise but it is hard to create, and the Government must take constructive action notwithstanding any criticism that may be brought against it.
I have shown what the enormous and far-flung activities of this tremendous railway system means to the Dominion of Canada; I have shown that it embraces over thirty companies, subsidiary and constituent; I have shown that it has 7,000 miles of completed line and 3,000 miles still to complete; I have shown numerous industrial companies in Canada are interested in its continuance-steel companies, rolling stock companies, manufacturing and other companies from Halifax to Vancouver-are	all interested in the
continuance of this great enterprise. It has involved itself with the very vitals of this country. Almost every province in Canada is upon its securities and concerned in its success. The Dominion of Canada has given no less than $58,000,000 of guarantees in connection with it, and between the Dominion and the provinces the people of Canada have paid over $20,000,000 in subsidies. I say that, having regard to this vast and complicated system, with its ramifications extending in every province of Canada, with the pressing demand of the West, as my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) knows, for more rolling stock, for better service, for extensions to the newer districts, with all these conditions, it is unthinkable that the Government should allow a system such as this to go into the hands of a receiver, if it can be saved. It is not a question of Mackenzie and Mann; it is a question of the interest of the people of Canada. For months past the Canadian Northern situation has troubled the money market of London, affecting adversely all Canadian securities and stopping the sources of supply of capital needed for our many enter-

prises. It has hung like a cloud over the business situation in Canada, just recovering from the terrible financial experience of last year. The most severe financial depression that has ever been known in my time we are now merging from; and in due course I hope to see the normal activities of the nation resumed, as we have reason to expect, on the experience and analogy of the past. The sooner that this situation is cleared up, the betteT for this and all other Canadian enterprises. I am speaking not only as a member of this Government; I am speaking as a Canadian and, I hope, as a patriot. I am satisfied that the sober business sense of this House and of this country will approve the proposals of the Government as the best solution of a trying and most difficult problem.

Mr. Speaker, I have some hesitation in following the hon. Minister of Finance in this debate; but I have followed his extended remarks on the financial side of this agreement, and I expected that he would deal with that side of the question, because there is no doubt that, as the Minister of Finance, he should have a wide knowledge of the financial features of this agreement. But what I would like to have heard and what the country would like to have heard from his lips is a statement as to the financial capacity of the Canadian Northern Railway Company and the financial abilities of the men behind that company, because that is more important to the people to-day than the financial terms of this agreement. The Minister of Finance says that the Government inherited the Canadian Northern difficulties. I think that when the Minister of Finance left the Liberal party, he was anxious to assume all the inheritance possible from that Government. During the time he was a member of the Liberal party,
I do not know that he ever offered advice to the members of that party that they should deal with the Canadian Northern railway in any other way than they did at that time. Yet he says to-day that we are responsible for the creation of this transcon- , tinental line. Conditions have changed in the last four years. During the time that the Liberal party in this country was dealing with the railroad problem, this country was developing very rapidly, and we were assured in 1911, as I understand it, that once the thirty-five million dollars was given to the Mackenzie and Mann interests, they would be able to complete their transcontinental railway, and

that no further requests would be made. Since that time the Conservative party has come into power and the Canadian Northern railroad has made demands every year and those demands have been yielded to. The country has gone through a crisis, as the hon. minister has mentioned. He says that we are merging from it. I come from western Canada and I see no signs whatever of an emergence from the crisis of 1913. I think we are in just as serious a financial crisis now as we were a year ago; and I do not see that this Government is doing anything to relieve the conditions which exist throughout this country at the present time and which have existed for the last year or two. But I say that the Government lacks foresight in continuing to follow a policy in western Canada that has caused more or less stagnation. That condition is one of the reasons why the railroads are finding it difficult to make their lines profitable and to continue the work of building new lines, and why this railway is finding it difficult to continue the construction of this particular line. The Minister of Finance finds himself and the Government confronted with a condition of their own making. If I were to place the credit for this particular arrangement, I would place the credit at the door of the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Bennett), and of the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. NicMe), Who have started a revolt against the Government and have indicated to them that the public demands that, if anything is given to the Canadian Northern railway, something should be given in return. If it had not been for that movement on the part of the supporters of the Conservative party, the Government would not have had any arrangement of this character to boast of, although it is one which is not satisfactory either to members on the Government side of the House or to the mass of the people of the country. But I believe the creation of the desire to have an arrangement with the Canadian Northern Railway Company was started by the movement within the party, by the knowledge that the people did not want any more trafficking with the Canadian Northern railway unless the country got something in return out of that particular road. I do not think, however, that this Government has gone about the matter in such a way as to get what they should have got out of the Canadian Northern railway.
Before going any further, I want to give credit to the position taken by my hon.
friend from Calgary, because be cQmes from a part of the country where railroads are in demand and where in the past we have made many sacrifices in order to get railway lines. I believe that the position taken by the hon. member for Calgary is the position of the western people. The Minister of Finance boasts of this partnership as though it were something to be proud of. I believe that the opinion of the people of this country is that there is nothing to be proud of in a partnership with Mackenzie and Mann or with the Canadian Northern railway, especially when it is a minor partnership in which we have no control over this concern owing to the amount of stock we hold. That is the objection I have to this partnership. I would rather have a partnership with the Grand Trunk railway, which is an old and respectable railroad corporation which has been in this country for years, and which has met the demands of the people to a very large extent. But, if I were to express my opinion of the Canadian Northern railway, and the way in which it has been financed, and the way in which its promoters have dealt with the people of this country, I do not think that my language would be parliamentary. The hon. member for Thunder Bay and Rainy River (Mr. Garrick) spoke of the hon. member for Calgary as a bucking broncho. As we know, bucking bronchos in the West are inclined to throw people; and I would not be a bit surprised that the attitude taken by the hon. member for Calgary and the hon. member for Kingston on this particular occasion would be very much the same as that of a bucking broncho, and that the Government might be thrown as a result of their particular policy on this question at this particular time.
I desire to state my views on this question as briefly as possible; but before doing so I would like to refeT to the assertion of the Finance Minister that the Canadian Northern railway cannot wait for this aid for six months. I believe that if this Parliament had met last fall and this demand had been made, it would have been considered as an urgent demand and that the help would have been needed at that time. There is no question that the demand has been made for the last six months, and the Canadian Northern is still in existence, still doing the same construction work and still creating more debts throughout this country. I think that the people of this country are prepared to accept a delay of six months if it will enable them to get



more accurate information as to the financial position of the Canadian Northern railway and of the men behind it. The men behind this railroad claim that they are almost bankrupt, and the Government joins with them as junior partner and lends its credit for $45,000,000 and takes $40,000,000 of stock in a concern controlled by two or three men who are, might I say, of the Get-rich-quick Wallingford type. I object as a citizen of this country and as a citizen of western Canada to this country being linked up as junior partner with men of that type. My view is this: That if we have to assist this railway and if further money is to be voted for the completion of the Canadian Northern system, the best way out of the difficulty is either control of the stock or complete ownership of the system by the people of Canada. We were reminded by the hon. member for Kingston in his speech the other evening of the policy in 1904 of the then leader of the Opposition, the present leader of the Government, when he declared in favour of government ownership of railways. He declared that that was a proper policy, and now when the opportunity comes for him to carry out the policy which he then believed in, he links the people of Canada up as junior partner with the Canadian Northern railway when he could just as well demand control and ownership of the road for the people of this country. This promise is very much like other promises which the leader of this Government has made; it is a promise made to the electors and a promise which he is not prepared to carry out when the party
10 p.m. which he leads comes into power. I say that if this country is to be a partner with this railroad, it should be a senior partner; if it can be only a junior partner, it is better for Canada that it should not be a partner at all.
I want to say something along the line of what I consider to be the public sentiment with regard to the men behind this particular railroad-and I believe that the members on the other side of the House realize this. The sentiment of the people of Canada is that the men who control the Canadian Northern railway have made vast fortunes; that individually they are in strong financial positions and that they are ambitious to control and possess, practically to own, a transcontinental road. The people of Canada believe that those men should sacrifice their private fortunes in the effort to realize their ambition. This Government has not established to the satis-

faction of any one in this House that the persons behind the Canadian Northern railway have made any attempt to sacrifice their interests in other large concerns in an effort to save this railroad. All they have done is to use their influence with this Government with a view to inducing them to take such steps as will save them and leave them in control of the stock of the company. Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann and others associated with the Canadian Northern railway have vast interests throughout this country, apart from the Canadian Northern railway. We know that they control the street railways of the cities of Toronto and Winnipeg. They control large coal mining interests on the Pacific coast and they are interested in large mines on the north shore of lake Superior. They are interested in the fisheries and in the timber of British Columbia. They have vast private holdings of real estate. They are interested in power companies and radial roads in the province of Ontario. They are interested in very large enterprises in Mexico and in Brazil.	The conclusion of the
people of Canada is that they should get rid of their other interests; and, if they want to	retain the Canadian
Northern railway and to save it from *bankruptcy, let them save it by using the financial interests which they have in other concerns throughout Canada, and throughout the North and Boutb American continents. That is my view, and I believe it is the popula'r view of the people of this country. Pressure should have been brought to bear on these men to force them to use all their private fortunes to save the road if they wanted to possess control of it, and if they would not do that, then if Canada was to give any assistance to the road, it should mean control and ownership of it. That is my position, and I desire to place it before the House, because I believe it is a position which represents the views of the majority of the people, at least of western Canada.
One feature of the arrangement proposed to be made by the Government with the Canadian Northern railway which is most disappointing to the people of western Canada is the fact that no provision is made for branch line construction. What we want in the West are branch lines, and in my view, if it was the intention to have a third transcontinental railway in this country, the Canadian Northern could have held back for some years the construction of that portion of their line

over the Eocky mountains to Vancouver. If they had devoted to the construction of branch lines in western Canada, the money which has been raised for the construction of that portion of the Transcontinental line, it would have been much better for this country, and would have meant a greater development of and probably more prosperity in western Canada. They might have waited until they had developed their branch line system, fed by the lines already constructed, and then, as they made that particular part of the system profitable, they would have been able to complete the main line to the Pacific coast by their own resources, practically without assistance from the people of Canada. I have had occasion in this House to point out the system under which the Canadian Northern operates with regard to projected branch lines in western Canada. I have told the House of the hardships which the men and women who have gone to that country have had to put up with by reason of the promises made year after year by the Canadian Northern Eailway people to build branch lines and their failure to carry them out. The head of the Canadian Northern railway is the best promiser in the country; but I do not know of a man who fails to carry out his promises to the same extent as Sir William Mackenzie. When we are sitting in this House, when Canadian Northern railway legislation is before us, we have many requests to assist that legislation. Me happen to be in control of things, and they come to us on bended knees and ask us to do certain things. Then they say what they will do in return. I am speaking now about the construction of lines. Last year I had occasion to see the head of the Canadian Northern railway and speak of the construction of a branch line which had been promised for a certain number of years into a country where people had been living and trying to develop land fifty, sixty and seventy miles away from a railway. I went to him and urged that something should be done to construct that particular line. His argument to me was: We have not the money, we are trying to get it-practically telling me that if I supported that particular measure, they would do something on that particular line. That might be the interpretation of his reply. I find that they got the money and did nothing whatever in regard to the construction of that particular line. What the people in my part of the country want to know from this Govern-2491
ment is:	With this $45,000,000, do they
intend to do something for the construction of branch lines where they are absolutely needed and have been promised for some years? That is the position I take on this particular question, which is a vital one with my people and with the people of southern Alberta. The head of the Canadian Northern railway is very anxious to meet our wishes when we were at Ottawa. But I want to point out the position taken by that gentleman when we are away from Ottawa. Petition after petition, signed by hundreds and hundreds of the people in that particular district, was presented to me. I forwarded these petitions to the president of the Canadian Northern railway. I happened to attend a demonstration there last July, 'between sixty and seventy miles away from any existing railroad. There were over 1,200 people in attendance at that particular demonstration and I think I can safely say that ninety per cent of them were fifty miles away from a railroad. They were in a district through which a Canadian Northern railway branch line that had been promised from year to year would go. I had ia photograph of that group taken which I sent to Sir William Mackenzie with a letter saying that these people were gathered in the part of the country which the Canadian Northern Eailway Lethbridge-Maryfield line would serve, 1,200 people, the majority of whom were fifty miles from a railway. I have not yet received an acknowledgment of either the photograph or the petitions. I point that out to show that the heads of the Canadian Northern railway are not showing any anxiety to serve the people of western Canada. The great anxiety they are showing is to complete a transcontinental road that will give distinction to Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann. I say that if they had abandoned the idea of completing a transcontinental railway, in so far as the line from Alberta through the Eockies to the Pacific coast is concerned, and had used the money devoted to that purpose to the construction of branch lines in Aloerta and Saskatchewan, they would have been serving the people of Canada much better than by the transcontinental railway proposition, which could have waited for a while. We have been told that branch lines may be completed under this arrangement. My own judgment and the judgment of other speakers who have opposed this particular agreement is that prac-

I do not propose at this time to go particularly into the figures that have been quoted so many times by members on both sides of the House, but for a little while I want to review this matter in a general way. The manner in which this bargain was put upon the table of the House in the resolution now before us, appeals to mv mind. I was very much struck by the speech of the hon. member for Centre Toronto (Mr. Bristol) in that nearly the whole plaint of it was that greater consideration should
be shown to Mackenzie and Mann. With that statement I entirely disagree. It appears to me that the history of the Canadian Northern railway since its inception, during the many yeaTs they have come to this House and to the legislatures and municipal and township councils of this Dominion, has been one long train of consideration shown to Mackenzie and Mann. The Canadian Northern railway has been practically fondled and petted and nursed up to what it is to-day. Therefore, when an hon. member asks the House to favourably consider this resolution because Mackenzie and Mann should receive some slight consideration, it does appear to me, with all due deference, that that argument ought not to hold water for a single moment, seeing that every consideration that could be shown to human beings has been given to Mackenzie and Mann for the carrying on of a project in which they never put a dollar of their own hard cash.
The one thing this House has to consider is whether or not this bargain is a good one. The Minister of Finance may, if he sees fit, split hairs on the question of partnership. I am not going to quarrel with him along those lines, hut, at any rate, there can be no partnership unless it is entered into for the sake of making profits; and from the information that has been laid on the table of the House it cannot very well be said to be a partnership because the Canadian Northern shows no profit at all in any of its branches. But it is a partnership in the sense that these two men in control of this great undertaking, with all its ramifications, have come to this House-as has been ably shown by the hon. member for Calgary, the hon. member for Kingston, and other members on this side of the House-and held up both hands and said: come and save us, without your aid we are absolutely gone. Therefore, the Government stands in the position of entering into a partnership with a concern that is "absolutely broken. The Government are the rich people coming to the aid of the Canadian Northern railway at the present moment, and the more they put into that railway the more they will have to put in, in order to save their necks. That is the whole story, in short. How good are the promises and the statements that have been made by these men in times gone by? If I mistake not, the Minister of Finance stood in the same place last year as he did to-night, and what did he say: Mackenzie and Mann want $15,000,000 of a cash gift;

give them that and the road will be completed. The words are hardly out of his mouth before Mackenzie and Mann come back, and this time they do not want $15,000,000, but three times $15,000,000. Again they say that the road will be completed. I do not believe that $45,000,000 will complete the road, and I propose to give figures in support of that to-night; and if $45,000,000 will not complete the road we are going to have the same spectacle in this House next year. Mackenzie and Mann will come back with the same old story, the same statements will be laid on the table of the House and information will be dragged up by the hair of its head just as it has been to-day.
Ah, this splendid Government, this far-seeing, astute Government, with all the acumen possessed by every one of its members, including the Solicitor General, have made a bargain with these people. A prominent part has been taken in this transaction by tlhe Solicitor General, and a great many of the wisest people in this Dominion are wondering how such a head could carry all the knowledge he possesses.
The argument that has been put up by the Minister of Finance, and the one argument that he seems to base his whole case on, is that you must not appoint a receiver. Nobody says you should appoint a receiver. It is not necessary to appoint a receiver. We do say that there should be control of the stock of the Canadian Northern, and that the allied companies should be given into the hands of the Government, that the Government should appoint a majority of the directors, persons who are actually railway men and not contractors, and that the money should be expended under their supervision. There is no necessity of a receiver. Nobody is anxious to see the Canadian Northern go to the wall. I do not want to see the Canadian Northern go to the wall, but I do want to see it managed as a railway ought to be, instead of the money being squandered here, there and everywhere, and perhaps devoted to purposes extraneous to the railway altogether.
Hon. gentlemen say that they are going to get stock and mortgages on stock as security, and that they cannot lose. Of what value are the stocks that have been offered to the Government by way of security? Does anybody know? We have only security upon one property, and that is the Brockville road, upon which we get a first mortgage. I defy Mackenzie and 
Mann to stand on the floor of this House and tell us how many mortgages and encumbrances there are on the rest of the stock offered to us. I do not believe they know, because I do not believe they have a proper system of audit in their business. Mackenzie and Mann told us last year that $15,000,000 would complete the road, and if they tell us this year that $45,000,000 will complete it, to my mind that is the best evidence that Mackenzie and Mann know not where they stand themselves. This action is being taken by the Government wholly on their say so. There is an agreement, they say, but it has been drawn by two of the most skilful lawyers in the city of Toronto, who have inserted conditions which ought not to have been agreed to. Mackenzie and Mann are handing over stocks, the value of which nobody knows, and they are getting from the people of Canada $45,000,000 in cash. How much have the people of Canada already contributed to this Canadian Northern railway?

From beginning to end the Canadian Northern railway has got out of the people of Canada, besides $70,000,000 from the rural municipalities, $337,100,000. Do they need consideration ? Do they need still to be nourished ? It only goes to show that if we had Mackenzie and Mann, practical railway men, as operators, and not as contractors, the road would have been completed and completed well, and the people of Canada would have been getting a return for the money that they had given to them. If you look at the list of securities which the Government is to get a mortgage upon, it would rather strike you that the Canadian Northern, coming and asking as they are, would give to the Government mortgages on all their assets. I am not talking of personal assets that they may have, but I should like to know why it is, that, when you look over the list of assets, contained in part 1 of the second schedule, the Toronto, Niagara and St. Catharines railway, a paying proposition, the Toronto, Niagara and Western railway, a paying

proposition, and the Inverness Railway and Coal Company, with a coal mine attached to it, a very paying proposition, are left out. Why is not the Government given the benefit of these securities and why is the Halifax and South Western left in which has never paid, and upon the bonds of which the Government has to pay $190,000 yearly interest P Why not put them all in ? Why not come, if you come at all, with clean hands ? Why not come here and say: We will give you such securities as you like but we will take ample care that the good ones are retained ? They are allowed to select the securities which they hand over to this all-wise Government with all its business acumen. Why does the Government not get the rest ? Does the Government, as a matter of fact, know today just what Mackenzie and Mann have and what they could give, or have Mackenzie and Mann simply come and said: We will give you this, you can take it; we must have the money, and the Government capitulate .and practically accept Mackenzie and Mann's terms ? That is exactly what happened.
What else happened P We advance the money and we take the securities. But this money that they are asking for will not complete the road. Then what happens ? We take on, by reason of the money that we are putting in, a present indebtedness upon the Canadian Northern amounting to $312,000,000. We have to stand behind it in order to save the money the people of Canada are putting in. But we have to put somebody to operate that road in order that the money may be got out of it by proper operation, something that Mackenzie and Mann have amply shown they are not able to do. We have to go on and practically take hold of the road and operate it in order that there may be a chance of getting our money back. When you consider the fact that the moneys that are to be advanced and have been advanced, represent a liability for every man, woman and child in Canada of $26, with ,a benefit coming back of only $5 in the shape of worthless sto ck, you realize exactly to what length the Government of this country has gone. They say that $45,000,000 will complete the road. Now, Sir, as you will see by looking at page 42 of the blue-book, their floating liabilities are $10,408,000; there is due on construction $21,262,000; there is balance for completion $41,905,000; there are amounts owing to the banks, $20,703,000; or, in other words, for completion these people need absolutely $94,279,000. Even, if as good a
mathematician as ini his own mind the Minister of Finance is, can show me where he can pay up $94,000,000 indebtedness with a paltry $45,000,000, then I will take off my hat to him as he did to the Solicitor General. The figures are there and they cannot be got away from. It will take, to complete the Canadian Northern railway, $94,279,000, and yet Mackenzie and Mann aire telling this Government, and this Government are attempting to tell the people of Canada, that $45,000,000 will complete the road. Why, it is the veriest buncombe; it is nothing more; it is nothing less. The Government know, and Mackenzie and Mann know better than the Government, that with this $45,000,000 they are dealing out one more sop to these raiilroad contractors, and the people of the country are getting in further and further, and that sooner or later they will have to take over the road and operate it themselves in order to save the money they have already put into it. The Government isay that the $40,000,000, with the right they would receive by reason of any default that may take place, is better than $51,000,000. I say that the right of default cannot come until after three years, because the Government has guaranteed the payment of the loans for that period, and in three years Mackenzie and Mann may have squandered the road over again and the $45,000,000 with it. Why should not the Government now take control themselves, and put iin a majority board of directors to operate that road? If the evil day is to come for the people of the	Dominion why	may not the
people of the Dominion just as well, have the evil day come now, rather than give more money to Mackenzie and Mann day after day and year after year as they are doing. There is no sense in {making two bites of a cherry in regard to this matter. By no method that the Finance Minister or the Solicitor General can devise can they 'make $45,000,000 do the work of $90,000,000, and by no method can you complete this Tailroad with the money that is now being given to it.
I repeat, Sir, that there ought to be a majority of this stock given to the people of Canada and that the people should operate the road. It is a well known fact that so far as Mackenzie and Mann are concerned, they are not railroad operators at all, and they admit that themselves. They are .Duraly contractors in every sense of the word, and the operation of a railroad is not

in their line at all. I say, Sir, that to allow men who have not put one single dollar of their own money into this enterprise to have control of this stock is an absolute breach of faith on the part of this Government, and in permitting it they are not standing Iby the interests of the people. We have had cited to us to-night the advances that were made in aid of the Canadian Pacific railway in years past, and the Minister of Finance told us he admired the courage of the men who built the Canadian Pacific railway. So does everybody admire their pluck, but it must not be forgotten that the men of the Canadian Pacific railway proved to the country the faith that was in them because they put up their own (money in it to as great an extent as they were able to, and they risked their all for that railroad. But far be it from Mackenzie and Mann to advance one single dollar of their own personal security, and in the agreement, as drawn with the Government, mighty good care is taken that Mackenzie and Mann should be clear so far as their personal securities are concerned.
In conclusion, I say, Sir, that the contract as drawn is not calculated to protect the interests of the people of Canada. I agree entirely with the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. R. B. Bennett) and the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle) and with those who have spoken bn this side of the House, that in so far as the figures go they show to a definite conclusion that these people are involved to such a hopeless extent that I doubt if they know just where they stand themselves. I say that Mackenzie and Mann in coming to this House to-day are absolutely groping in the dark; they are asking for $45,000,000 knowing they will get it and knowing well that all they will have to do is to come back again and another advance will be made by this Government because the money already invested in the road-will have to be protected. That is my belief,-and I say, therefore, and I cannot say it too strongly, that so far as this agreement is concerned it is bad from beginning to end. I say that Mackenzie and Mann are in all probability getting something for nothing. Again, I repeat, that in only one of those securities do we get a first mortgage, and that the securities taking them all in all are of no intrinsic value whatever. Mackenzie and Mann are not putting a five cent piece of their own money into the venture. They are afraid themselves to come m wJiere they ask the people of Canada to

enter. They have not the courage of their own convictions, and before one single dollar is given them under this resolution Mackenzie and Mann should be told in the strongest tones: if you say that $45,000,000 will complete the road; if you believe that the road when completed will be a paying proposition, then show your own faith in it by pledging your own securities, do not ask the people of Canada to get in and assume the whole load which is almost too heavy to bear now, while you, Mackenzie and Mann, keep out there and save your own hides; at least have the courage of men and show your own faith in the proposition.
